topics.t: What is business? Meaning, role and features
topics.h: A chaiwala at Pune station, Tata Steel and a two-person app startup look nothing alike, yet all three are doing the same thing: business.
p: Economic activities are done to earn a living (money); non-economic activities are done out of love, sentiment, religion or social duty, e.g. a mother cooking for her family or volunteering at a flood camp.
Business is an economic activity involving the regular production or purchase and sale of goods and services with the aim of earning profit.
Features of business: an economic activity; production or procurement of goods/services; sale or exchange; dealings on a regular basis; profit earning; uncertainty of return; element of risk.
A one-time sale (selling your old cycle once) is not business, because regularity is missing. Making goods only for self-use is not business, because there is no sale or exchange.
Business drives development: it produces goods and services, creates jobs and incomes, generates wealth and taxes, and pushes innovation.

ex.q: Meena bakes cakes for her daughter's birthday every year. Her neighbour Farhan bakes cakes every day and sells them to cafés. Who is doing business?
st: Check the motive: Meena bakes out of love (non-economic); Farhan bakes to earn money (economic).
Check sale or exchange: only Farhan sells.
Check regularity: Farhan sells daily; Meena bakes once a year, for the family.
Farhan meets all the features; Meena's baking lacks the profit motive, the sale and regular dealings.
ex.a: Only Farhan is carrying on business.

topics.rl: When Indian two-wheeler makers expanded plants in places like Hosur and Pantnagar, local suppliers, transporters and eateries grew around them: one business creating jobs and income for many others.

rv.summary: Business is an economic activity of regularly producing or buying and selling goods and services to earn profit, with uncertain returns and risk. It differs from non-economic activity, which is done out of love or duty.
focus: Telling economic from non-economic activities using the motive
The seven features of business: economic activity, production or procurement, sale or exchange, regularity, profit, uncertainty of return, risk
Spotting the missing feature in cases like a one-time sale or goods made for self-use
The role of business in jobs, incomes, wealth, taxes and innovation
remember: Business: regular production or purchase and sale of goods and services with the aim of earning profit
One-time sale = no regularity; production for self-use = no sale or exchange
traps: Don't call a one-time sale business: regularity is missing
A guaranteed, fixed return is not a feature of business; returns are uncertain
Don't label work as non-economic just because it is a service: a salaried nurse is doing economic activity

topics.t: Trade in ancient India: routes, transport, centres and guilds
topics.h: Long before container ships docked at Mundra, Indian cotton and pepper were sailing to Rome and caravans were carrying Indian goods across Central Asia.
p: Ancient India traded by land and by sea. Overland routes such as the Silk Route linked India with China, Central Asia and the West; sea routes linked Indian ports with the Arabian world, East Africa, Rome and South-East Asia.
Transport: roads and caravans by land; rivers and coastal shipping by water. Monsoon winds helped sailors time their voyages across the Arabian Sea.
Merchant guilds (shreni) were associations of traders or craftsmen. They framed rules for members, settled disputes, fixed standards and protected members' interests: a form of self-regulation.
Major trade centres: Pataliputra, Taxila, Mathura, Varanasi, Ujjain, Peshawar and Indraprastha inland; ports such as Surat, Broach (Bharuch), Tamralipti and Kaveripatnam (Puhar).
Ports linked regions: Tamralipti in Bengal looked east, Kaveripatnam was a port of the Chola kingdom in the south, and Surat and Broach on the west coast traded with West Asia and beyond.

ex.q: Project idea: you are making a chart of ancient trade centres for your class. Where would you place Tamralipti, Kaveripatnam and Surat on an outline map of India?
st: Tamralipti: on the east coast in Bengal, a gateway for trade with the east.
Kaveripatnam (Puhar): on the south-east coast near the mouth of the Kaveri, in the Chola kingdom.
Surat: on the west coast in Gujarat, a great port in the Mughal period.
Add arrows for the goods traded and the regions they reached.
ex.a: East coast (Bengal): Tamralipti; south-east coast (Tamil Nadu): Kaveripatnam; west coast (Gujarat): Surat.

topics.rl: Today the Sagarmala programme and new ports along the coast echo India's old maritime story; the same west-coast region that once hosted Broach and Surat is again a trade hub.

rv.summary: Ancient India traded by land routes like the Silk Route and by sea using monsoon winds, through inland centres and ports. Merchant guilds called shrenis regulated their own members.
focus: Land and sea routes, and how monsoon winds helped sailors
The role of shrenis: rules, disputes, standards, self-regulation
Locating ports: Tamralipti (Bengal), Kaveripatnam (Chola), Surat and Broach (west coast)
Telling inland centres (Ujjain, Taxila, Mathura, Varanasi) from ports
remember: Shreni = guild of merchants or craftsmen
Tamralipti: Bengal, east
Kaveripatnam (Puhar): Chola port, south
Surat and Broach: west coast
traps: Don't call Ujjain or Pataliputra a port: they were inland centres
Don't place Kaveripatnam in Bengal; it was a Chola port in the south
Don't confuse a shreni with a hundi: one is a guild, the other a credit instrument

topics.t: Indigenous banking: hundi, chitti and intermediaries
topics.h: Centuries before UPI, a trader in Surat could send money to a merchant in Varanasi on a piece of paper called a hundi, and people trusted it.
p: Indigenous bankers and moneylenders (sahukars, seths) accepted deposits, lent money and financed trade long before modern banks.

Hundi: an indigenous credit instrument, a written order to pay money, used to finance trade and remit funds. It was negotiable, i.e. it could be transferred from one person to another. Chitti was another document used in such dealings.

Kinds of hundi: Dhani-jog (payable to any person, no responsibility over who receives payment); Shah-jog (payable to a specific, respectable person whose identity is required); Firman-jog (payable to order); Jokhmi (drawn against dispatched goods; if the goods are lost in transit, the drawee is not liable).
Intermediaries such as commission agents, brokers and distributors grew in importance. They financed trade and bore risks, linking producers with distant buyers.

ex.q: A cloth merchant sends a hundi drawn against a consignment of cotton bales. The bales are lost in a shipwreck. Which hundi is this, and who bears the loss?
st: The hundi is tied to goods in transit, so it is a Jokhmi hundi.
Under a Jokhmi hundi the drawee pays only if the goods arrive safely.
The goods were lost, so the drawee has no liability.
ex.a: Jokhmi hundi; the drawee is not liable, and the loss falls on the drawer or holder.

topics.rl: The idea of the hundi survives in the bill of exchange and the cheque. Brokers on Dalal Street are modern intermediaries in the same tradition.

rv.summary: Indigenous bankers financed trade using hundis, negotiable written orders to pay money, of kinds like Dhani-jog, Shah-jog, Firman-jog and Jokhmi. Intermediaries such as agents and brokers financed trade and bore risks.
focus: The meaning of hundi and why it was negotiable
The four kinds of hundi and who gets paid under each
Why Jokhmi hundi frees the drawee if goods are lost
The role of commission agents, brokers and distributors
remember: Dhani-jog: payable to any person
Shah-jog: payable to a specific respectable person
Firman-jog: payable to order
Jokhmi: drawn against goods; drawee not liable if goods are lost in transit
traps: Don't mix up Dhani-jog (anyone) and Shah-jog (an identified respectable person)
Don't think the drawee must pay under a Jokhmi hundi when goods are lost
A hundi is a credit instrument, not a guild or a tax

topics.t: Goods traded and India's place in the world economy
topics.h: Pepper from Malabar was so prized abroad that it was nicknamed 'black gold'. How did India go from trade giant to colony and back to a fast-growing economy?
p: Major exports of ancient India: spices, textiles (cotton and muslin), indigo, sugar, gems and pearls, ivory and other animal products.
Major imports: horses, gold and silver (precious metals), wine, silk from China, coral and tin.
For centuries the Indian subcontinent was one of the largest economies in the world and a major source of manufactured goods like fine textiles.
Under colonial rule India declined: it became a supplier of raw materials and a market for British factory goods, and local crafts and industries suffered.

After Independence India built an industrial base; the economic reforms of 1991 (liberalisation, privatisation, globalisation) opened the economy, and India re-emerged as one of the fastest-growing major economies.

ex.q: Sort these into ancient exports and imports: indigo, horses, spices, gold, muslin, wine.
st: India had a surplus of agricultural and craft products: indigo, spices, muslin.
India lacked good war-horses and precious metals and imported them along with wine.
Exports: indigo, spices, muslin. Imports: horses, gold, wine.
ex.a: Exports: indigo, spices, muslin. Imports: horses, gold, wine.

topics.rl: Indian spices, textiles and gems are still major export items today, while India imports gold and crude oil: some patterns have lasted for two thousand years.

rv.summary: Ancient India exported spices, textiles, indigo, sugar and gems and imported horses, gold, silver and wine. Once a top world economy, it declined under colonial rule and re-emerged after the 1991 reforms.
focus: Sorting goods into ancient exports and imports
Why gold and silver flowed into India
How colonial rule turned India into a raw-material supplier and market for British goods
The 1991 reforms: liberalisation, privatisation, globalisation
remember: Exports: spices, textiles (cotton, muslin), indigo, sugar, gems, pearls, ivory
Imports: horses, gold, silver, wine, silk from China, coral, tin
1991 reforms = LPG
traps: Indigo was an export, not an import
Don't think India became a big economy only after 1991; it was one for centuries before colonial rule
Colonial rule hurt Indian crafts; it did not expand them

topics.h: A chartered accountant, a bank clerk and a sweet-shop owner may all earn well, but the way they start, work and earn is completely different.
p: Profession: an occupation requiring specialised knowledge and training, where entry is restricted by a professional body and members follow a code of conduct. Examples: doctors, lawyers, chartered accountants.
Employment: an occupation in which a person works for others and gets a salary or wages, under a service contract or rules. Example: a bank clerk.

Establishment: business by the entrepreneur's decision (plus legal formalities if needed); profession by membership of a professional body and certificate of practice; employment by appointment letter and service agreement.

Reward: business earns profit; profession earns professional fee; employment earns salary or wages. Capital: business needs capital as per size; profession needs limited capital; employment needs none.

Risk: high in business (uncertain profits), some in profession (fees fairly regular), little in employment (fixed pay). Transfer of interest is possible only in business. Code of conduct: none prescribed for business; professional code for professions; employer's norms for employees.

ex.q: Dr Kavita runs her own clinic, Arjun works as a software engineer at a company, and Harpreet owns a dhaba. Classify each and state their reward.
st: Dr Kavita has a medical degree and registration, and renders expert service: profession, reward = professional fee.
Arjun works for an employer under a contract: employment, reward = salary.
Harpreet sells food regularly for profit with her own capital: business, reward = profit.
ex.a: Kavita: profession (fee); Arjun: employment (salary); Harpreet: business (profit).

topics.rl: To practise as a chartered accountant in India you must become a member of the ICAI and follow its code of ethics; that is exactly what makes it a profession.

rv.summary: Business, profession and employment differ in how they start, the reward, the capital needed, the risk, transfer of interest and code of conduct. Profit, fee and salary are their rewards.
focus: Comparing the three occupations on establishment, reward, capital, risk, transfer and code of conduct
Classifying a person's present occupation from a case
Why professions follow a code of conduct
remember: Reward: business = profit; profession = professional fee; employment = salary or wages
Start: business = owner's decision; profession = membership and certificate of practice; employment = appointment letter
Risk: high in business, some in profession, little in employment
traps: Don't classify by qualification alone: a lawyer working on a salary is in employment
Transfer of interest is possible only in business
Don't say employment has no code: employees follow the employer's norms

topics.h: From a coal mine in Jharkhand to a car plant in Chennai to a cold-storage chain in Punjab, every business falls into either industry or commerce.
p: Business activities are classified into two broad groups: industry (producing or processing goods and services) and commerce (distributing them).

Primary industries: extractive (draw products from natural sources, e.g. mining, farming, fishing, lumbering, hunting) and genetic (rear and breed plants and animals for reproduction, e.g. plant nurseries, poultry farms, cattle breeding, fish hatcheries).

Secondary industries use primary output to make further goods. Manufacturing has four types: analytical (separates materials into parts, e.g. oil refinery), synthetical (combines ingredients into a new product, e.g. cement), processing (successive stages, e.g. sugar, paper) and assembling (puts components together, e.g. cars, computers, TVs). Construction (roads, dams, buildings) is also secondary.
Tertiary or service industries provide support services such as transport, banking, insurance, warehousing, communication and advertising. They help primary and secondary industries.

ex.q: A company crushes limestone, mixes it with clay and gypsum and produces cement. Another separates crude oil into petrol, diesel and kerosene. Identify each type.
st: Cement: several ingredients are combined into one new product, so it is synthetical.
Crude oil: one material is broken into different products, so it is analytical.
ex.a: Cement: synthetical industry; oil refinery: analytical industry.

topics.rl: A Kolhapur sugar mill (processing), a Gurugram car plant (assembling), an Odisha mine (extractive) and a Namakkal poultry farm (genetic) together show the whole range of Indian industry.

rv.summary: Industry produces or processes goods: primary (extractive and genetic), secondary (manufacturing of four kinds, and construction) and tertiary (support services). Commerce distributes them.
focus: Telling extractive from genetic industry
The four kinds of manufacturing: analytical, synthetical, processing, assembling
Placing construction under secondary and services like warehousing under tertiary
remember: Extractive: mining, farming, fishing
Genetic: nurseries, poultry, cattle breeding, fish hatcheries
Analytical: oil refinery; Synthetical: cement; Processing: sugar, paper; Assembling: cars, TVs
traps: Don't call a fish hatchery extractive: breeding is genetic
Don't confuse analytical (splits one material) with synthetical (combines ingredients)
Construction is secondary, not tertiary

topics.t: Commerce: trade and auxiliaries to trade
topics.h: Darjeeling tea is grown in the hills, but you drink it in Kanyakumari months later. Commerce is the bridge that makes this possible.
p: Commerce = trade + auxiliaries to trade. It covers all activities needed to move goods from producers to consumers.
Commerce removes hindrances: of person (trade links buyer and seller), place (transport), time (warehousing), risk (insurance), finance (banking) and information (advertising and communication).
Trade means buying and selling. Internal trade is within a country: wholesale (in large quantities) and retail (in small quantities to final consumers).
External trade is between countries: import (buying from abroad), export (selling abroad) and entrepot (importing goods in order to re-export them).
Auxiliaries to trade are support services: transport and communication, banking and finance, insurance, warehousing, and advertising.

ex.q: A Mumbai firm imports electronic parts from Taiwan and re-exports them to Kenya. Which type of trade is this, and which auxiliaries would it need?
st: Goods are imported only to be sent abroad again, so this is entrepot trade.
Ships move the goods (transport), banks handle payments (finance), insurers cover the cargo (insurance), and goods may wait in a port warehouse (warehousing).
ex.a: Entrepot trade; it needs transport, banking, insurance and warehousing.

topics.rl: Cold-storage warehouses in Uttar Pradesh let potatoes harvested in February reach kitchens in October: warehousing removing the hindrance of time.

rv.summary: Commerce is trade plus auxiliaries to trade. Trade is internal (wholesale, retail) or external (import, export, entrepot), and auxiliaries remove the hindrances of person, place, time, risk, finance and information.
focus: Matching each auxiliary to the hindrance it removes
Types of trade: internal (wholesale, retail) and external (import, export, entrepot)
Telling auxiliaries apart from industries like mining
remember: Commerce = trade + auxiliaries to trade
Person: trade; place: transport; time: warehousing; risk: insurance; finance: banking; information: advertising
Entrepot = import for re-export
traps: Don't match warehousing with place; it removes the hindrance of time
Mining is an industry, not an auxiliary to trade
Wholesale trade within India is internal, not external, trade

topics.h: If profit were the only goal, why would a company spend crores on research, training and clean technology? Because a business needs many objectives to survive.
p: Profit is essential: it is a source of income, a source of finance for growth, a measure of efficiency, a reward for risk and a builder of reputation. It is needed for survival and growth.

But profit cannot be the only objective. Peter Drucker's key areas: market standing, innovation, productivity, physical and financial resources, earning profits, manager performance and development, worker performance and attitude, and social responsibility.
Market standing = position relative to competitors. Innovation = new ideas or methods. Productivity = output compared with input.

Economic objectives: profit, growth, market standing, innovation, productivity. Social objectives: quality goods at fair prices, fair wages and good working conditions, employment, protecting the environment and community welfare.

ex.q: Which key-area objective is a firm pursuing when it compares output per worker with last year's and tries to improve it?
st: Output compared with input measures productivity.
Improving output per worker is improving productivity.
ex.a: Productivity.

topics.rl: Indian two-wheeler makers have chased market standing in rural India for decades, while also investing in innovation such as electric scooters.

rv.summary: Profit is essential for income, growth, efficiency and as a reward for risk, but a business also pursues market standing, innovation, productivity and other key areas, plus social objectives.
focus: Why profit is needed and why it cannot be the only objective
Drucker's key areas and their meanings
Telling economic objectives from social objectives
remember: Market standing = position relative to competitors
Innovation = new ideas or methods
Productivity = output compared with input
Profit: income, finance for growth, measure of efficiency, reward for risk, reputation
traps: Employment generation is a social objective, not an economic one
Don't treat profit as the only objective of business
Lowering taxes is not one of Drucker's key areas

topics.t: Business risk: nature, causes and kinds
topics.h: A weak monsoon, a sudden strike or a new rival app: any of these can wipe out a firm's profit overnight. That possibility of loss is business risk.
p: Business risk is the possibility of inadequate profits or even losses due to uncertainties or unexpected events.
Nature: risks arise from uncertainties; risk is an essential part of every business; the degree of risk depends mainly on the nature and size of business; profit is the reward for risk taking.

Causes: natural (floods, earthquakes, drought, lightning); human (dishonesty or negligence of employees, strikes, riots, management inefficiency); economic (changes in demand, prices, competition, technology, interest rates, failure to collect dues); other (political disturbances, mechanical failures such as a boiler bursting, exchange-rate changes).
Speculative risk has the possibility of both gain and loss (e.g. changes in prices or demand). Pure risk has only the possibility of loss or no loss (e.g. fire, theft, strike).

ex.q: A rice exporter worries that (i) the rupee may rise and cut his earnings and (ii) his godown may catch fire. Classify each risk by cause and kind.
st: Exchange-rate change: an 'other' cause; it may cause gain or loss, so it is speculative.
Fire: a natural or accidental cause; it can only cause loss, so it is pure risk.
ex.a: (i) Exchange-rate change: speculative risk; (ii) fire: pure risk.

topics.rl: Farm-equipment and fertiliser companies watch IMD monsoon forecasts closely, because a bad monsoon is a natural cause of risk for their sales.

rv.summary: Business risk is the possibility of low profits or losses due to uncertainty. It arises from natural, human, economic and other causes, and may be speculative (gain or loss) or pure (loss only).
focus: The nature of business risk and its link with profit
Classifying causes as natural, human, economic or other
Telling speculative risk from pure risk
remember: Speculative risk: chance of gain or loss (price, demand changes)
Pure risk: loss or no loss (fire, theft, strike)
Exchange-rate change, political disturbance, mechanical failure = other causes
traps: Theft and fire are pure risks, not speculative
Don't call an exchange-rate change an economic cause here; the lesson lists it under 'other causes'
Insurance cannot remove all business risk

topics.h: Two friends in Indore want to launch a cloud-kitchen. Before cooking a single biryani, they must make about ten big decisions.
p: Selection of line of business: what to produce or sell, based on market demand and expected profit.
Size of the firm: depends on the scale of demand, available finance and technology. Choice of form of ownership: sole proprietorship, partnership, company and so on.
Location: near raw materials, labour, market, transport and banking facilities.
Financing the proposition: estimate fixed and working capital and plan sources. Physical facilities (machines, building, utilities) and plant layout (physical arrangement of facilities).
Competent and committed workforce; tax planning (tax laws affect many decisions); and finally launching the enterprise by mobilising resources and starting operations.

ex.q: A cement maker chooses to build its plant near limestone mines rather than near a big city. Which basic factor is it deciding, and why?
st: The decision is about where to set up, so it is the location factor.
Cement uses bulky raw material, so being near limestone cuts transport costs.
ex.a: Location of the business, chosen to be close to raw material.

topics.rl: Many Indian startups now register through government portals and plan GST registration early, because tax planning is part of starting right.

rv.summary: Starting a business means deciding the line of business, size, form of ownership, location, finance, physical facilities and layout, workforce and tax planning, and then launching the enterprise.
focus: The list of basic factors in starting a business
Matching a case to its factor, e.g. location or plant layout
Why location and tax planning need care at the start
remember: Plant layout = physical arrangement of facilities
Financing = estimating fixed and working capital and planning sources
Launching the enterprise is the final step
traps: Don't confuse location (where) with plant layout (arrangement inside)
Dividend policy is not a basic start-up factor
The first decision is the line of business, not launching

topics.t: Forms of organisation and the sole proprietorship
topics.h: The paan shop near your school and Reliance Industries are both businesses, but who owns them, who is liable and who decides are completely different questions.
p: A form of business organisation is the type of ownership and management structure of a business. Main forms in India: sole proprietorship, Joint Hindu Family business, partnership, cooperative society and joint stock company.
Sole proprietorship: a business owned, managed and controlled by one individual, who is the recipient of all profits and the bearer of all risks.
Formation and closure are easy, with few legal formalities (a licence may be needed for some trades). There is no separate law governing it.
Liability is unlimited: if business assets fall short, the owner's personal assets can be used to pay business debts.

Sole risk bearer and profit recipient; full control with the owner; no separate legal entity from the owner; and lack of business continuity, since death, illness or insanity of the owner can end the business.

ex.q: Suresh's hardware shop owes ₹5,00,000 to suppliers but its assets are worth only ₹3,00,000. What happens to the remaining ₹2,00,000?
st: A sole proprietor has unlimited liability.
Creditors can recover this from Suresh's personal assets, such as his car or savings.
ex.a: Suresh must pay ₹2,00,000 from his personal assets.

topics.rl: Most kirana stores, tailoring shops and small repair centres across India are sole proprietorships: easy to start and run by one person's drive.

rv.summary: A sole proprietorship is owned, managed and controlled by one person who gets all profits and bears all risks. It is easy to form, has unlimited liability, no separate legal entity and no continuity.
focus: The features: one owner, easy formation, unlimited liability, sole risk bearer, full control
Why there is no separate legal entity and no business continuity
Applying unlimited liability to a shortfall case
remember: Sole proprietorship: owned, managed and controlled by one individual
Unlimited liability: personal assets can pay business debts
No separate law governs it; a licence may be needed for some trades
traps: Perpetual succession is a company feature, not of a sole proprietorship
Don't think the owner and business are separate in law
Liability is not limited to the capital in the business

topics.h: Why do lakhs of Indians still choose to run their business alone, even though it means unlimited liability?
p: Merits: quick decision making (no one to consult); confidentiality of information (no need to share or publish accounts); direct incentive (all profits go to the owner); sense of accomplishment (personal satisfaction); ease of formation and closure.

Limitations: limited resources (only owner's savings and borrowings); limited life of the business (lack of continuity); unlimited liability (owner's personal assets at risk); limited managerial ability (one person cannot be expert in everything).
Because of these limits, sole proprietorship suits businesses that are small, need personal attention and have limited capital needs, such as local shops and beauty parlours.
As the business grows, owners often move to partnership or company form to get more capital and skills.

ex.q: Pooja runs a successful bakery alone. She wants to open five more outlets but her bank will lend only a small amount. Which limitation is she facing, and what could she do?
st: She depends on her own savings and limited borrowings, so it is the limitation of limited resources.
To raise more funds and share the work, she could take partners or form a company.
ex.a: Limited resources; she could convert to a partnership or company to raise more capital.

topics.rl: A Lucknow chikan embroidery shop run by one owner can change designs the same day a trend appears: quick decision making in action.

rv.summary: A sole proprietorship offers quick decisions, secrecy, direct incentive, satisfaction and easy formation, but suffers from limited resources, limited life, unlimited liability and limited managerial ability.
focus: Matching each merit to its cause, e.g. quick decisions from not consulting anyone
The four limitations and their effects
Which businesses suit this form and when to move to partnership or company
remember: Merits: quick decisions, confidentiality, direct incentive, sense of accomplishment, ease of formation and closure
Limitations: limited resources, limited life, unlimited liability, limited managerial ability
traps: Don't list limited liability or perpetual succession as merits of sole proprietorship
Direct incentive is not a government subsidy; it means all profit goes to the owner
Big projects like steel plants do not suit this form

topics.h: In some family businesses, a newborn baby becomes a member the day she is born. Welcome to the Joint Hindu Family business.
p: A Joint Hindu Family (HUF) business is owned and carried on by members of a Hindu Undivided Family. It is governed by Hindu Law; the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 applies to inheritance.
Basis of membership is birth in the family. Members are coparceners. The eldest member, called the karta, manages the business.

Two systems: Dayabhaga (prevails in West Bengal) and Mitakshara (rest of India). NCERT notes that under Dayabhaga both male and female members can be coparceners, while Mitakshara traditionally allowed only males; the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 made daughters coparceners too.

Features: formation needs at least two members and ancestral property; no agreement needed; liability of karta is unlimited, others' liability is limited to their share in the property; karta controls the business; continuity: on the karta's death the next eldest becomes karta; minors can be members.

Merits: effective control, continued business existence, limited liability of members, increased loyalty and cooperation. Limitations: limited resources, unlimited liability of karta, dominance of karta, limited managerial skills.

ex.q: The karta of an HUF business dies. His eldest son is 40 and his granddaughter is 6. What happens to the business?
st: An HUF business does not end on the death of the karta.
The next eldest member becomes the karta and continues the business.
The 6-year-old granddaughter remains a member because membership is by birth.
ex.a: The business continues; the next eldest member becomes karta, and the minor stays a member.

topics.rl: Many traditional trading families in Indian markets still keep their accounts and property as an HUF, which is also recognised separately for income tax.

rv.summary: A Joint Hindu Family business is run by members of a Hindu Undivided Family under Hindu Law. Membership is by birth, the eldest member (karta) manages with unlimited liability, and others have limited liability.

Liability: karta unlimited, other coparceners limited to their share
Dayabhaga (West Bengal) and Mitakshara (rest of India)
Merits and limitations, especially continuity and karta's dominance
remember: Karta = eldest member who manages the business
Dayabhaga: West Bengal; Mitakshara: rest of India

traps: Don't give the karta limited liability: his liability is unlimited

topics.t: Partnership: meaning, features, merits and limitations
topics.h: Two engineering friends pool their savings and skills to start a robotics workshop. The moment they agree to share profits, a partnership is born.
p: The Indian Partnership Act, 1932 defines partnership as the relation between persons who have agreed to share the profits of a business carried on by all or any of them acting for all.

Features: formation by agreement (oral or written); liability is unlimited, and joint and several; risk bearing and profits shared; decision making and control by partners jointly; continuity is restricted (death, retirement, insolvency or insanity of a partner can end it); minimum 2 members, maximum 50 (the Companies Act, 2013 lets the government prescribe a limit of up to 100, and the Companies (Miscellaneous) Rules, 2014 currently fix it at 50); mutual agency.
Mutual agency: every partner is both an owner and an agent of the firm; an act of one partner binds all.
Merits: ease of formation and closure; balanced decision making; more funds; sharing of risks; secrecy.
Limitations: unlimited liability; limited resources (members restricted); possibility of conflicts; lack of continuity; lack of public confidence (accounts are not published).

ex.q: Asha and Vikram are partners. Vikram, acting for the firm, buys ₹2,00,000 of raw material on credit without telling Asha. Is Asha bound?
st: Partnership has mutual agency: each partner is an agent of the firm.
Vikram acted in the course of the firm's business.
So his act binds the firm and Asha too.
ex.a: Yes, Asha is bound because of mutual agency.

topics.rl: Many CA and law firms and family textile businesses in Surat run as partnerships, pooling capital and skills of a few trusted people.

topics.h: A famous cricketer lets a sports shop use his name as 'partner' but puts in no money. If the shop goes bust, can creditors come after him? Yes!
p: Active partner: contributes capital, takes part in management, shares profits, has unlimited liability, and is known to outsiders.

Sleeping (dormant) partner: contributes capital and shares profits, but does not take part in management; unlimited liability; not known to outsiders. Secret partner: takes part in the business but his association is kept secret from outsiders; unlimited liability.

Nominal partner: lends only his name; no capital, no management, no share in profits, but liable to third parties. Partner by estoppel: by his own words or conduct gives the impression that he is a partner; liable to third parties who deal on that basis. Partner by holding out: declared a partner by the firm and does not deny it after knowing, so becomes liable.

Minor: cannot be a full partner but can be admitted to the benefits of partnership with the consent of all partners; his liability is limited to his share; he cannot take part in management; on becoming major he must decide within six months whether to become a partner.

By duration: partnership at will (no fixed period; continues at the will of partners) and particular partnership (for a specific project or period; ends on its completion). By liability: general partnership (unlimited liability of all partners) and limited partnership (at least one partner with unlimited liability). A Limited Liability Partnership (LLP, under the LLP Act, 2008) is a separate legal entity in which partners' liability is limited.

ex.q: Karan, a famous actor, allows a firm to use his name on its board as 'partner' but invests nothing and takes no profit. A supplier sells goods on credit trusting his name. What type of partner is Karan, and is he liable?
st: He lends only his name: no capital, no management, no profit share.
That makes him a nominal partner.
Nominal partners are liable to third parties who give credit believing they are partners.
ex.a: Nominal partner; yes, he is liable to the supplier.

topics.rl: Many startups and consultancies in India register as LLPs to get partnership flexibility with limited liability.

rv.summary: Partners may be active, sleeping, secret, nominal, by estoppel or by holding out, and a minor may be admitted to benefits. Partnerships may be at will or particular, general or limited, and an LLP gives limited liability.

topics.h: Friends fall out over money more often than over anything else. A partnership deed puts the rules in writing before the arguments begin.
p: Partnership deed: the written agreement setting out the terms of partnership. The agreement among partners may even be oral, but a written deed (on stamp paper) is preferred because it avoids disputes.

Usual contents: name of the firm; nature and location of business; duration; capital contributed by each partner; profit-sharing ratio; duties and obligations of partners; salaries and drawings; interest on capital and drawings; terms for admission, retirement and expulsion; preparation of accounts and audit; method of settling disputes; procedure for dissolution.

Registration of a partnership is optional under the 1932 Act, but non-registration has consequences: a partner of an unregistered firm cannot sue the firm or other partners; the firm cannot sue third parties; and the firm cannot sue its partners. Third parties can still sue the firm.

Procedure: submit an application in the prescribed form to the Registrar of Firms (with name and location of the firm, names of other places of business, date of joining of each partner, names and addresses of partners and duration), signed by all partners; pay the fee; the Registrar enters the firm in the Register of Firms and issues a certificate of registration.

ex.q: An unregistered firm supplied goods worth ₹1,50,000 to a customer who refuses to pay. Can the firm file a suit? Can the customer sue the firm if the goods were defective?
st: Non-registration bars the firm from suing third parties.
So the firm cannot file a suit to recover ₹1,50,000.
But third parties are not barred; the customer can sue the firm.
ex.a: The firm cannot sue the customer; the customer can sue the firm.

topics.rl: Registering a firm in India is done with the state's Registrar of Firms, often online; many banks ask for the registration certificate before opening a firm's current account.

topics.h: Lakhs of dairy farmers in Gujarat each own a tiny herd, yet together they built Amul. That is the power of cooperation.
p: A cooperative society is a voluntary association of persons who join together to protect their common economic interests. It must be registered under the Cooperative Societies Act, 1912 or the relevant State Cooperative Societies Act; at least ten adult members are needed.

Features: voluntary membership (free to join and leave); legal status (separate entity after registration); limited liability (to the capital contributed); control by an elected managing committee on 'one member, one vote'; service motive rather than profit.

Merits: equality in voting status; limited liability; stable existence (not affected by death or insolvency of members); economy in operations (members often offer honorary services, middlemen are removed); support from government; ease of formation.

Limitations: limited resources; inefficiency in management (cannot pay high salaries to professionals); lack of secrecy; government control (rules, audits, reports); differences of opinion among members.

Types: consumer (buys directly from producers to eliminate middlemen), producer (supplies raw materials and tools to small producers), marketing (pools members' output and sells at the best price), farmers' (helps farmers gain from large-scale farming), credit (gives loans at low interest, protecting members from moneylenders), cooperative housing (helps people with limited income build houses at reasonable cost).

ex.q: Fifty small weavers in Varanasi want (i) yarn and looms at fair prices, and later (ii) to sell their sarees jointly at a good price. Which types of cooperatives suit each need?
st: Need (i) is about getting inputs for production: producer's cooperative.
Need (ii) is about pooling and selling output: marketing cooperative.
ex.a: (i) Producer's cooperative; (ii) marketing cooperative.

topics.rl: Primary agricultural credit societies give small loans to farmers in villages across India, protecting them from high-interest moneylenders.

topics.t: Joint stock company: meaning, features, merits and limitations
topics.h: Infosys has lakhs of shareholders, yet in a court case it appears as just one name. The company is a person in the eyes of law, an 'artificial' one.
p: A company is an association of persons formed for carrying on business, having a legal status independent of its members. It is governed by the Companies Act, 2013.

Features: artificial person (created by law; can own property, sue and be sued); separate legal entity from its members; formation through a lengthy legal process; perpetual succession (members may come and go, the company continues); control by the elected board of directors; limited liability of members; common seal as the official signature (made optional by a 2015 amendment); risk borne by shareholders in proportion to their investment.

Merits: limited liability; transfer of interest (shares can be transferred, easily in a public company); perpetual existence; scope for expansion (large capital from many investors, borrowing ability); professional management.

Limitations: complexity in formation; lack of secrecy (many reports filed and published); impersonal work environment; numerous regulations; delay in decision making; oligarchic management (a few directors control); conflict of interests among shareholders, directors, employees and creditors.

ex.q: Arun owns 1,000 shares of ₹10 each, fully paid, in a company that goes bankrupt with huge debts. What is the most he loses?
st: Liability of shareholders is limited to the unpaid amount on their shares.
His shares are fully paid: 1,000 × ₹10 = ₹10,000 invested.
Creditors cannot touch his personal assets.
ex.a: At most ₹10,000, the amount he invested.

topics.rl: When a big Indian company's founder passes away, the company still continues its operations without interruption. That is perpetual succession.

topics.t: Private, public and One Person Companies
topics.h: Why does one company's name end in 'Private Limited', another's in 'Limited', and a third's in '(OPC) Private Limited'?
p: Private company: restricts the right of members to transfer shares; limits the number of members to 200 (excluding present and past employees who are members); prohibits any invitation to the public to subscribe to its securities. Minimum 2 members and 2 directors. Must use 'Private Limited' after its name.

Privileges of a private company: can be formed with just 2 members and 2 directors; no need to issue a prospectus; allotment of shares without waiting for minimum subscription; fewer compliance requirements.

Public company: any company that is not a private company. Minimum 7 members, no maximum; minimum 3 directors; shares freely transferable; can invite the public to subscribe. A private company that is a subsidiary of a public company is treated as a public company.

One Person Company (OPC): a company with only one person as member, introduced by the Companies Act, 2013. It has a separate legal entity and limited liability; it needs a nominee who will become member if the owner dies or is incapacitated; 'One Person Company' is written in brackets below its name; minimum 1 director.

ex.q: A company has 230 members, of whom 40 are current employees holding shares. It does not invite the public and restricts share transfers. Can it remain a private company?
st: Employee members are excluded from the 200 limit.
Members counted = 230 − 40 = 190.
190 ≤ 200, and the other conditions are met.
ex.a: Yes. Counting only 190 members, it stays within the private company limit.

topics.rl: Many family-run Indian businesses start as 'Pvt Ltd' companies and later become public 'Ltd' companies through an IPO on the NSE or BSE.

rv.summary: A private company has 2–200 members, restricts share transfer and cannot invite the public; a public company needs 7 members and 3 directors. An OPC has one member, limited liability and a nominee.

topics.t: Formation of a company: stages and the promoter
topics.h: Every company, from a tiny tech startup to a giant steel maker, begins with someone who spots an idea and pushes it into existence: the promoter.
p: Formation of a company goes through stages: promotion, incorporation and (for a public company raising money from the public) capital subscription before it starts business.
Promotion is the first stage: conceiving a business opportunity and taking steps to form a company. The person who does this is the promoter.

Functions of a promoter: identifying the business opportunity; feasibility studies (technical, financial and economic); name approval (applying to the Registrar of Companies); fixing up signatories to the Memorandum of Association; appointment of professionals (bankers, auditors, legal advisers); preparation of necessary documents (MoA, AoA, consent of directors and others).
Incorporation: the company is registered with the Registrar of Companies, who issues a certificate of incorporation, and the company comes into legal existence.

ex.q: Neha wants to start a solar-panel company. She checks if the technology works, whether the project will be profitable and whether there is demand. Which promoter function is this?
st: Checking technology = technical feasibility.
Checking profitability = financial feasibility.
Checking demand and economic viability = economic feasibility.
ex.a: Feasibility studies (technical, financial and economic).

topics.rl: Founders of Indian startups typically check name availability on the government's company registration portal first: name approval is a classic promoter step.

topics.h: If a company formed to run hospitals suddenly starts selling cars, is that legal? The answer lies in its 'constitution': the Memorandum of Association.
p: Memorandum of Association (MoA): the most important document, defining the company's objects and its relationship with the outside world. Clauses: name clause, registered office clause, objects clause, liability clause, capital clause and association (subscription) clause.
A company cannot legally do anything beyond the objects in its MoA; such acts are 'ultra vires' and void, and cannot be ratified even by all shareholders.

Articles of Association (AoA): rules for the internal management of the company. The AoA is subordinate to the MoA and must not go against it. Acts beyond the AoA but within the MoA can be ratified by shareholders.

Other documents filed for incorporation: consent of proposed directors; agreement with the proposed managing director, if any; statutory declaration that all legal requirements have been complied with; payment of fees.

The Registrar of Companies issues a certificate of incorporation, which is conclusive evidence that the company has been legally formed. Under the 2013 Act, a Corporate Identity Number (CIN) is allotted.

ex.q: A company's MoA allows it to make garments. Its directors use company funds to start a film production unit. Is the act valid? Can shareholders ratify it?
st: Film production is outside the objects clause of the MoA.
Acts beyond the MoA are ultra vires and void.
Such acts cannot be ratified even by all shareholders.
ex.a: Invalid (ultra vires); it cannot be ratified.

topics.t: Choosing the right form of business organisation
topics.h: A street-food stall, a CA firm, a milk union and an electric-car maker all chose different forms. Their choices weren't random; they followed clear factors.
p: Factors in choosing a form: cost and ease of setting up; liability (unlimited vs limited); continuity; management ability; capital considerations; degree of control; nature of business.

Cost and ease: sole proprietorship is cheapest and easiest; a company is costliest and most complex. Liability: unlimited for sole proprietors, partners and the karta; limited for cooperative members and company shareholders.

Continuity: companies and cooperatives have stable or perpetual existence; sole proprietorships and partnerships lack it. Control: complete in sole proprietorship; shared in partnership; separated from ownership in a company.

Capital: large and growing needs suit the company form; small needs suit sole proprietorship or partnership. Nature of business: direct personal contact (e.g. tailoring) suits sole proprietorship; large manufacturing suits a company; professional services suit partnership.
Project idea: interview a local shop or firm owner, find out its form of ownership, why it was chosen and its pros and cons, and present it to your class.

ex.q: Ritu wants to start a business needing huge capital, with limited risk to her personal assets, which should continue even after her retirement. Which form suits her best?
st: Huge capital: needs many investors, so a company.
Limited personal risk: limited liability, so a company.
Continuity after her retirement: perpetual succession, so a company.
ex.a: Joint stock company.

topics.t: India's mixed economy: private and public sectors
topics.h: You may travel on a government-run train, pay with a private bank's app and buy a snack made by a cooperative, all in one trip. That is India's mixed economy.
p: India follows a mixed economy, in which the private sector and the public sector exist side by side.
Private sector: enterprises owned by individuals or groups of individuals, such as sole proprietorships, partnerships, Joint Hindu Family businesses, cooperatives and companies.
Public sector: enterprises owned, managed and controlled by the central government, a state government or both, either wholly or partly.
The government decides the role of each sector through its industrial policies; public enterprises can take the form of departmental undertakings, statutory corporations or government companies.

ex.q: Classify: (a) Indian Railways, (b) a Pune software firm owned by two friends, (c) Steel Authority of India Limited.
st: Indian Railways is run by the Ministry of Railways: public sector.
The software firm is owned by private individuals: private sector.
SAIL is owned mainly by the Government of India: public sector.
ex.a: (a) Public, (b) private, (c) public.

topics.rl: India's skies show the mix too: airports are run by the public Airports Authority of India and also by private operators under concession agreements.

topics.h: Indian Railways has its own minister in the Union Cabinet. That tells you how it is organised: as a department of the government.
p: Departmental undertakings are enterprises set up as departments of a ministry and are considered part of the government. Examples: Indian Railways, the Department of Posts, defence production units.

Features: funded by annual appropriations from the government's budget and revenue goes to the treasury; subject to the accounting and audit controls applicable to government activities; employees are government servants recruited under government rules; a part of the ministry with no separate legal entity; directly controlled by and accountable to the ministry.
Merits: effective control by Parliament; high degree of public accountability; revenue goes to the treasury; most suitable where national security or strategic control is involved.

Limitations: lack of flexibility; delays in decisions due to bureaucracy (red tape); undue political interference; civil servants may lack business experience; often insensitive to consumer needs; unable to take advantage of business opportunities.

ex.q: The government wants an enterprise to make sensitive defence equipment under the direct watch of the ministry and Parliament. Which form suits it, and why?
st: Strategic and security concerns need tight government control.
A departmental undertaking is directly under the ministry and accountable to Parliament.
ex.a: Departmental undertaking, because it allows close government control where national security is involved.

topics.rl: India Post runs as a department of the Ministry of Communications, so major decisions on postal services pass through the ministry.

topics.h: LIC was born on the pages of an Act passed by Parliament in 1956. That 'birth by statute' gives it a special mix of government power and business freedom.
p: Statutory corporations are public enterprises brought into existence by a Special Act of Parliament or a state legislature. The Act defines their powers, functions, rules, employees and relationship with government. Examples: Life Insurance Corporation of India (LIC Act, 1956), Food Corporation of India (Food Corporations Act, 1964).
They are described as having the power of the government and the operational flexibility of private enterprise.

Features: set up under an Act; separate legal entity that can sue, be sued, own property and enter contracts; wholly owned by the state, with the government having ultimate financial responsibility; usually independently financed through borrowings from government or the public and revenue from sales; employees are not civil servants; not subject to the budget, accounting and audit procedures of government departments.

Merits: independence in functioning and high operational flexibility; government generally does not interfere in financial matters; framed by Parliament, so it has a clear legal framework; it can be a valuable instrument for economic development combining public interest with business efficiency.

Limitations: in practice, operational flexibility is limited and government or political interference in major decisions is common; where public money is involved, misuse and corruption may occur; any change in its constitution requires amending the Act by Parliament.

ex.q: The government wants to set up a public enterprise with a clear legal identity, autonomy in finance and recruitment, but answerable to Parliament. Which form suits it?
st: A clear legal identity and autonomy point to a separate legal entity with flexibility.
Accountability to Parliament comes from being created by a Special Act.
That combination is a statutory corporation.
ex.a: Statutory corporation.

topics.rl: The Food Corporation of India, set up by a 1964 Act, buys grain from farmers and stores and distributes it across India for the public distribution system.

topics.h: BHEL, SAIL and HAL all end with 'Limited'. They are companies like any other, except that the government holds the majority of their shares.
p: A government company is a company in which not less than 51% of the paid-up share capital is held by the central government, or by one or more state governments, or partly by the central government and partly by state governments. A subsidiary of a government company is also a government company. Examples: BHEL, SAIL, Hindustan Aeronautics Limited.

Features: registered under the Companies Act, 2013; separate legal entity that can sue, be sued and own property; management regulated by the Companies Act and its articles; employees appointed under the company's own rules; funds come from the government and other shareholders, and it can raise money from the capital market.
Merits: easy to establish (only Companies Act requirements); separate legal entity; autonomy in management decisions; can control the market and curb unhealthy business practices.

Limitations: where the government is the only shareholder, Companies Act provisions have little relevance; it evades constitutional responsibility because it is not directly answerable to Parliament like a department; management and administration rest with the government, which may interfere.

ex.q: Of a company's paid-up capital of ₹100 crore, the central government holds ₹40 crore and a state government holds ₹15 crore. Is it a government company?

55% ≥ 51%, and central plus state holdings can be added.
ex.a: Yes, it is a government company (55% held by governments).

topics.h: Department, corporation or company? A board-exam favourite: read the case, spot the clues, name the form.

Legal entity: none for a department; separate entity for both corporation and company.
Finance: department from the budget; corporation from the government plus its own borrowings and revenue; company from government and private shareholders, and the capital market.

Employees: civil servants in a department; the corporation's own rules; the company's own rules. Accountability: department to the ministry; corporation to Parliament through the Act; company to its board and shareholders, with the government as main shareholder.

So it is a statutory corporation.

topics.t: Changing role of the public sector
topics.h: In the 1950s the government built steel plants itself. Today it sells shares in some public enterprises. Why the change?
p: Original role after Independence: development of infrastructure (heavy industry, power, transport); regional balance (setting up units in backward areas); economies of scale (in industries needing huge investment); check over concentration of economic power in a few private hands; import substitution (self-reliance by producing goods at home).
The New Industrial Policy of 1991 changed the approach to make public enterprises efficient and competitive.

Reduction in the number of industries reserved for the public sector, opening them to private firms; today only a couple of strategic areas, such as atomic energy and railway operations, remain reserved.
Disinvestment: selling part of the government's equity in public enterprises to private investors and the public, to improve efficiency and raise resources.

Policy on sick units: sick public enterprises were referred to the Board for Industrial and Financial Reconstruction (BIFR) to decide on revival or closure (BIFR was abolished in 2016; such cases now go to the National Company Law Tribunal under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016). Memorandum of Understanding (MoU): an agreement between the government and a public enterprise that gives management more autonomy while holding it accountable for agreed targets.

ex.q: The government sells 10% of its shares in a profitable public enterprise through the stock exchange. Which post-1991 policy measure is this, and what does it aim at?
st: Selling government-held shares to the public is disinvestment.
It aims to bring in private ownership and market discipline, improve efficiency and raise funds.
ex.a: Disinvestment, aimed at improving efficiency and raising resources.

topics.rl: Steel plants at Bhilai, Rourkela and Durgapur were set up by the public sector partly to develop backward regions: the 'regional balance' role in action.

rv.summary: After Independence the public sector built infrastructure, balanced regions, gained scale, checked concentration of power and replaced imports. Since 1991, reservations were cut and disinvestment, sick-unit reform and MoUs were introduced.
focus: The five original roles of the public sector
The 1991 changes: fewer reserved industries, disinvestment, policy on sick units, MoUs
Why heavy industry was taken up by the public sector
remember: Disinvestment: selling part of government equity to private investors and the public
MoU: autonomy for management + accountability for targets
Sick units went to BIFR; since 2016, NCLT under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code
traps: Disinvestment reduces, not increases, government shareholding
Regional balance is not the same as import substitution
Only a couple of strategic areas, such as atomic energy and railway operations, remain reserved

topics.h: The phone in your pocket may be designed in one country, assembled in another and sold in a hundred more. The firms that run such networks are global enterprises.
p: Global enterprises (multinational corporations, MNCs) are huge industrial organisations that extend their operations across many countries through branches, subsidiaries and networks. They pursue a global strategy and are controlled from their headquarters.

Features: huge capital resources (and ability to raise funds from many sources); foreign collaboration (agreements on technology, brands and patents with local firms); advanced technology; product innovation (strong research and development); marketing strategies (aggressive and effective, building global brands); expansion of market territory (operations spread across borders); centralised control (headquarters in the home country controls the branches and subsidiaries).
MNCs bring investment, technology and jobs to host countries, but they can also outcompete local firms because of their size.

ex.q: A carmaker headquartered in Japan has plants in India, Thailand and Mexico, all following product and pricing policies set by the head office. Which feature of global enterprises does this show?
st: Operations in many countries = expansion of market territory.
Policies decided by the head office = centralised control.
ex.a: Expansion of market territory with centralised control by headquarters.

topics.rl: Maruti Suzuki is a well-known example of foreign collaboration: Suzuki of Japan brought technology and design to an Indian partner.

rv.summary: Global enterprises (MNCs) are huge firms operating across many countries under a global strategy, with huge capital, foreign collaboration, advanced technology, product innovation, strong marketing and centralised control.

The seven features and matching each to a case
Effects of MNCs on host countries
remember: Features: huge capital, foreign collaboration, advanced technology, product innovation, marketing strategies, expansion of market territory, centralised control
Centralised control: head office controls branches
traps: Branches of an MNC are not fully independent; control is central
MNCs are not limited to one country
Foreign collaboration is about agreements with local firms, not centralised control

topics.h: Many new highways and airport terminals in India were built neither by the government alone nor by a private company alone, but by both together.
p: Joint venture (JV): two or more independent firms pool resources and expertise for a common purpose, usually forming a new entity. Partners share ownership, control, profits and risks.

Benefits of JVs: increased resources and capacity; access to new markets and distribution networks; access to technology; innovation; low cost of production (e.g. using local labour and materials); established brand name of a partner.

Public-private partnership (PPP): a model in which tasks, obligations and risks are allocated between public and private partners in an optimal way. The government provides support such as land, policy and funding; the private partner brings capital, expertise and efficient operations.

Features of PPP: used in sectors such as power, roads, ports, airports, water and sanitation, hospitals and schools; government handles social obligations and regulation, private partner is responsible for efficiency; revenue or profits are shared as agreed.

ex.q: An Indian company with a strong rural distribution network partners with a foreign company that has advanced battery technology to make electric scooters. What benefits does each gain?
st: Indian partner gains access to technology and innovation.
Foreign partner gains access to new markets and an established distribution network.
Both share resources, costs and risks.
ex.a: Indian firm: technology; foreign firm: market access and distribution; both: shared resources and risk.

topics.rl: Several Indian airports and expressways are developed under PPP, where the government provides land and approvals while private developers build and operate them.

rv.summary: A joint venture is two or more firms pooling resources for a common purpose and sharing ownership, control, profits and risk. In a PPP, the government and a private partner share tasks, obligations and risks.

What the government and the private partner each bring in a PPP
Sectors where PPP is used

PPP: government gives land, policy, funding and handles social obligations; private partner brings capital, expertise, efficiency
traps: In PPP the government, not the private partner, handles social obligations
Market access and technology access are different JV benefits
PPP is used for big infrastructure, not small shops

topics.h: You can take a packet of biscuits home, but you cannot take home a haircut or a train ride. Services are different from goods in five important ways.
p: Services are intangible, essential activities that satisfy needs. Goods are tangible products that can be seen, touched and stored.

Five Is of services: Intangibility (cannot be touched; the experience matters); Inconsistency (quality varies each time and with each customer); Inseparability (production and consumption happen together); Inventory (less) (services cannot be stored for later); Involvement (the customer takes part in the delivery).

Goods vs services: tangible vs intangible; goods are fairly homogeneous, services are heterogeneous; goods can be stored, services cannot; ownership of goods passes to the buyer, but services give only an experience; goods can be returned, services cannot.

Business services are used by firms to conduct activities: banking, insurance, transportation, warehousing and communication. Social services are provided voluntarily for social goals, e.g. NGOs offering health care or education. Personal services are experienced differently by each customer, e.g. tourism, recreation, restaurants.

ex.q: An empty seat on a flight that took off this morning cannot be sold tomorrow. Which feature of services does this show?
st: The seat-service existed only for that flight's time.
It could not be stored and sold later.
This is the feature of no inventory.
ex.a: Inventory (less): services cannot be stored.

topics.rl: IRCTC cannot store today's unsold train berths for next week: every journey is a perishable service.

rv.summary: Services are intangible activities that satisfy needs. Their five Is are intangibility, inconsistency, inseparability, inventory (less) and involvement. They may be business, social or personal services.
focus: Matching a case to one of the five Is
Differences between goods and services
Classifying business, social and personal services
remember: Five Is: Intangibility, Inconsistency, Inseparability, Inventory (less), Involvement
Business services: banking, insurance, transport, warehousing, communication
traps: Don't confuse inseparability (made and used together) with involvement (customer takes part)
Services give an experience, not ownership
An empty flight seat can't be stored and sold later: that is inventory (less)

topics.h: Your monthly pocket money, your father's home loan and the cheque your aunt sends on your birthday all pass through one institution: the bank.
p: A bank accepts deposits of money from the public for the purpose of lending or investment, repayable on demand or otherwise, and withdrawable by cheque, draft or order (as per the Banking Regulation Act, 1949).

Types of banks: commercial banks (public sector, where the government holds the majority, and private sector); cooperative banks (under state cooperative laws, giving cheap credit to members); specialised banks (foreign exchange banks, industrial banks, development banks, export-import banks); and the central bank (the Reserve Bank of India, which supervises and regulates banks and controls money supply).

Functions of commercial banks: accepting deposits; lending of funds (loans, overdraft, cash credit, discounting of bills); cheque facility (bearer and crossed cheques); remittance of funds (bank drafts, pay orders, electronic transfers); allied services (bill payments, lockers, buying and selling shares, underwriting).
Banks earn mainly from the difference between the interest they charge on loans and the interest they pay on deposits.

ex.q: A bank pays 6% interest per year on deposits of ₹10,00,000 and lends the whole amount at 10% per year. What is its gross interest margin for the year?
st: Interest earned = 10% of 10,00,000 = ₹1,00,000.
Interest paid = 6% of 10,00,000 = ₹60,000.

topics.rl: The State Bank of India is a public sector bank, HDFC Bank is a private sector bank, and the RBI regulates both.

rv.summary: A bank accepts deposits from the public for lending or investment. Banks are commercial, cooperative, specialised or central (RBI). Commercial banks take deposits, lend, give cheques, remit funds and offer allied services.
focus: The Banking Regulation Act definition of a bank
Types of banks and the role of the RBI
The five functions of commercial banks
How banks earn from the interest gap
remember: Bank: accepts deposits for lending or investment, withdrawable by cheque, draft or order
Remittance: drafts, pay orders, electronic transfers
Bank income = interest on loans − interest on deposits
traps: The RBI does not take savings deposits from the public
Lockers are an allied service, not a lending function
Don't call a bank with majority government shares a private bank

topics.h: A college student, a supermarket owner and a retired teacher all need very different bank accounts. Picking the wrong one means losing either interest or convenience.
p: Savings account: encourages savings by individuals; earns interest; limits on withdrawals may apply. Current account: for businessmen, with no limit on the number of transactions; usually no interest; overdraft facility possible.

Recurring deposit (RD): a fixed amount deposited every month for a fixed period; earns higher interest than savings. Fixed deposit (FD): a lump sum deposited for a fixed period; earns higher interest; penalty on premature withdrawal.

Multiple option deposit account: a savings account in which the amount above a set limit is automatically transferred into a fixed deposit, and FDs are broken automatically when the savings balance is insufficient, so the customer gets both liquidity and higher interest.

Remittance: a bank draft is an order by a bank to its branch (or another bank) to pay a specified sum, used to send money to another place; a pay order (banker's cheque) is used for payment within the same city.

Overdraft: a current-account holder may withdraw more than his balance up to a sanctioned limit; interest is charged only on the amount overdrawn. Cash credit: the bank sanctions a cash loan limit against security of current assets (such as stock); interest is charged on the amount actually used.

ex.q: Kiran has an overdraft limit of ₹1,00,000 on her current account with ₹20,000 balance. She issues a cheque of ₹70,000. How much is overdrawn, and on what amount is interest charged?
st: Balance available = ₹20,000.
₹50,000 is within the ₹1,00,000 limit.
Interest is charged only on the overdrawn ₹50,000.
ex.a: ₹50,000 overdrawn; interest is charged on ₹50,000.

topics.rl: Many Indian banks offer 'sweep-in' accounts: the modern version of the multiple option deposit account.

rv.summary: Banks offer savings, current, recurring, fixed and multiple option deposit accounts, remit funds through drafts and pay orders, and lend through overdraft and cash credit, charging interest only on the amount used.
focus: Choosing the right account for a case
Drafts (outstation) vs pay orders (same city)
Overdraft vs cash credit and on what amount interest is charged
remember: Current account: unlimited transactions, usually no interest, overdraft possible
RD: fixed monthly sum; FD: lump sum for a fixed period
Overdraft and cash credit: interest only on the amount actually used
traps: Interest is not charged on the whole sanctioned limit
A pay order is for the same city, not for foreign remittance
Overdraft is linked to a current account; cash credit is against security of current assets

topics.h: Your parents may remember standing in long bank queues to send money. Today it takes seconds on a phone. That revolution is e-banking.
p: E-banking (electronic banking) means using the internet, mobile phones and electronic networks to carry out banking transactions. It is also called internet or online banking.

Services: Electronic Fund Transfer (EFT); National Electronic Funds Transfer (NEFT), which settles transfers in batches; Real Time Gross Settlement (RTGS), which settles each transaction individually and instantly, generally for large amounts; Automated Teller Machines (ATMs); debit cards (money is deducted from the account at once); credit cards (spending on credit up to a limit, paid later); internet and mobile banking.

Benefits to customers: banking 24 hours a day, 365 days a year; transactions from anywhere (office, home, while travelling); a record of every transaction, giving financial discipline; greater customer satisfaction.
Benefits to banks: competitive advantage; unlimited network, not limited by the number of branches; less load on branches because of centralised databases.

ex.q: A company must pay a large amount to a supplier immediately and wants each payment settled individually in real time. Which service should it use?
st: Real time = settled at once, not in batches.
Gross settlement = each transaction settled individually.
Large-value urgent transfers suit RTGS.
ex.a: RTGS (Real Time Gross Settlement).

topics.rl: UPI and net banking let a kirana owner in a small town pay a wholesaler in Mumbai at midnight, something impossible when branches were the only option.

rv.summary: E-banking uses the internet and electronic networks for banking, through EFT, NEFT, RTGS, ATMs, debit and credit cards and mobile banking. It gives customers 24×7 access and gives banks an unlimited network.
focus: NEFT (batches) vs RTGS (individual, real time)
Debit card vs credit card
Benefits to customers vs benefits to banks
remember: RTGS: each transaction settled individually and instantly, usually large amounts
NEFT: settled in batches
Debit card: deducted at once; credit card: pay later up to a limit
traps: Don't say NEFT settles in real time
24×7 access is a benefit to customers; less branch load is a benefit to banks
E-banking is not limited to branch hours

topics.h: A vegetable seller in your colony now has a QR code taped to her cart. India's digital payment story has reached every street corner.
p: Digital payments are payments made through digital or online modes, with no physical exchange of cash.

Banking cards (debit, credit and prepaid cards); USSD (Unstructured Supplementary Service Data), using *99# for banking on basic phones without internet; AEPS (Aadhaar Enabled Payment System), for transactions using Aadhaar authentication at micro ATMs or with business correspondents.

UPI (Unified Payments Interface): links multiple bank accounts into one mobile app for instant transfers using a virtual payment address; developed by the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI).
Mobile wallets: store money digitally on a phone for quick payments; bank prepaid cards: loaded in advance with a fixed amount.

Point of Sale (PoS) terminals: card-swiping or tap machines at shops; internet banking and mobile banking; micro ATMs: small devices used by business correspondents to provide basic banking in remote areas.

ex.q: A farmer in a village has a basic phone without internet and wants to check his balance and transfer money. Which digital mode suits him?
st: No internet rules out UPI apps and internet banking.
USSD works on basic phones by dialling *99#.
ex.a: USSD (*99#) banking.

topics.rl: UPI, developed by NPCI, is used everywhere from chai stalls to big malls; India now records billions of UPI transactions every month.

rv.summary: Digital payments involve no physical cash. Modes include banking cards, USSD (*99#), AEPS, UPI, mobile wallets, prepaid cards, PoS terminals, internet and mobile banking and micro ATMs.
