What UPI, USSD and AEPS mean
PoS terminals vs micro ATMs
remember: USSD: *99#, basic phones without internet
AEPS: Aadhaar Enabled Payment System
UPI: by NPCI; many bank accounts in one app, virtual payment address
traps: Don't suggest UPI apps when there is no internet: use USSD
A prepaid card cannot be spent beyond its loaded amount
Micro ATMs are used by business correspondents, not shop checkouts

topics.h: A thousand shopkeepers each pay a small amount; when fire hits one shop, the pool pays for the damage. That simple idea of pooling risk is insurance.
p: Insurance is a contract in which one party (the insurer) agrees, in return for a consideration (the premium), to compensate the other party (the insured) for loss caused by specified risks. The document is the policy.
It works on pooling of risk: many people facing a similar risk contribute premiums to a common fund, from which the few who suffer loss are paid.

Functions: providing certainty (of payment against uncertain loss); protection (against loss from the event, though not against the event itself); risk sharing (loss is shared by all who pay premiums); assisting in capital formation (premiums collected are invested in productive activities).
Insurance does not prevent fire or accidents; it only reduces their financial impact.

ex.q: 2,000 shop owners each pay a premium of ₹1,500 into an insurance pool. In a year, fire damage to some shops totals ₹25,00,000. Is the pool enough to pay the losses?
st: 30,00,000 > 25,00,000, so the pool can pay all claims.
ex.a: Yes. The pool of ₹30,00,000 covers losses of ₹25,00,000.

topics.rl: LIC invests a large share of the premiums it collects in government securities and infrastructure: insurance helping capital formation.

rv.summary: Insurance is a contract where the insurer, for a premium, compensates the insured for loss from specified risks. It works on pooling of risk and provides certainty, protection, risk sharing and capital formation.
focus: Insurer, insured, premium and policy
Pooling of risk
The four functions of insurance
remember: Insurance: insurer compensates the insured for loss from specified risks, in return for premium
Functions: certainty, protection, risk sharing, capital formation
traps: Insurance does not prevent fire or accidents
The premium is paid by the insured, not the insurer
Investing premiums is capital formation, not risk sharing

topics.h: A shopkeeper insures his goods worth ₹5 lakh with two companies and expects ₹10 lakh after a fire. Seven principles of insurance explain why he won't get it.
p: Utmost good faith (uberrimae fidei): both parties must disclose all material facts honestly. Insurable interest: the insured must have a financial interest in the subject matter, i.e. he suffers a loss if it is damaged.
Indemnity: the insurer compensates only the actual loss, up to the sum insured; the insured cannot profit from insurance. It applies to fire and marine insurance, not to life insurance.
Proximate cause (causa proxima): when loss results from two or more causes, the nearest (most direct) cause decides whether the loss is covered.
Subrogation: after paying the claim, the insurer takes over the insured's rights over the damaged property (e.g. salvage) and against third parties.

Contribution: if the same property is insured with more than one insurer, they share the loss in proportion to the sums insured; the insured cannot recover more than the actual loss. Mitigation: the insured must take reasonable steps to minimise loss, like an uninsured person would.

ex.q: Goods worth ₹6,00,000 are insured with Insurer A for ₹4,00,000 and Insurer B for ₹2,00,000. Fire causes a loss of ₹3,00,000. How much does each insurer pay?
st: By contribution, loss is shared in that ratio.
By indemnity, the insured gets exactly ₹3,00,000, no more.
ex.a: A pays ₹2,00,000 and B pays ₹1,00,000.

topics.rl: After a car is written off in an accident and the insurer settles the claim, the insurer takes the wreck and can recover from the guilty party: that is subrogation.

rv.summary: Insurance follows seven principles: utmost good faith, insurable interest, indemnity, proximate cause, subrogation, contribution and mitigation. The insured can never recover more than the actual loss.
focus: Matching a case to the right principle
Applying indemnity and contribution to a loss
Why indemnity does not apply to life insurance
remember: Utmost good faith: disclose all material facts
Indemnity: actual loss only, up to sum insured
Subrogation: insurer takes over the insured's rights after paying
Contribution: insurers share loss in ratio of sums insured
traps: Don't pay the full sum insured when the loss is smaller
Indemnity does not apply to life insurance
Subrogation is not the same as contribution

topics.h: Life insurance is often called 'life assurance' because death is certain; only its timing is not.
p: Life insurance: a contract in which the insurer, in return for premium, agrees to pay a sum on the death of the insured or on the expiry of a fixed period, whichever is earlier, depending on the policy. It is a contract of protection and investment, not of indemnity.
Elements: it is a valid contract; utmost good faith; insurable interest at the time of taking the policy; it is not a contract of indemnity; the amount is paid on death or maturity.

Policies: whole life (sum paid only on death of the insured, to beneficiaries); endowment (sum paid at maturity, or on earlier death); joint life (two or more lives insured, usually spouses or partners; sum paid on the first death to the survivor(s)); annuity (sum paid in instalments after the insured reaches a certain age); children's endowment (for children's education or marriage, paid when the child reaches a certain age).

Health insurance covers medical and hospital expenses due to illness or injury. With rising medical costs, it protects families from large unexpected bills; many policies offer cashless treatment at network hospitals.

ex.q: Anil, 35, wants a policy that pays him a lump sum at 55 to fund his retirement, but pays his family if he dies before 55. Which policy suits him?
st: Payment at maturity (age 55) or on earlier death = endowment policy.
ex.a: Endowment policy.

topics.rl: Government schemes such as Ayushman Bharat-PMJAY provide health cover to crores of families, showing how important health insurance is in India.

rv.summary: Life insurance pays a sum on death or at maturity and is a contract of protection and investment, not indemnity. Policies include whole life, endowment, joint life, annuity and children's endowment. Health insurance covers medical costs.
focus: The elements of life insurance
Matching a need to the right policy
Why life insurance is not a contract of indemnity
Why health insurance matters
remember: Whole life: paid only on death
Endowment: paid at maturity or on earlier death
Joint life: two or more lives; paid on first death
Annuity: instalments after a certain age
traps: Don't confuse whole life (death only) with endowment (maturity or earlier death)
Insurable interest in life insurance is needed at the time of the policy, not at death
Life insurance is not a contract of indemnity

topics.t: Fire and marine insurance; comparing the three
topics.h: A ship carrying Indian basmati to the Gulf faces storms and pirates; the godown storing it faces fire. Different risks need different insurance.
p: Fire insurance: the insurer agrees, for a premium, to compensate the insured for loss or damage to property from fire during a specified period, up to the sum insured. Elements: insurable interest both at the time of contract and at the time of loss; utmost good faith; indemnity; the loss must be caused by actual fire (or flame); the fire must be accidental, not intentional; proximate cause.

Marine insurance covers risks of sea voyages. Hull insurance covers the ship (vessel); cargo insurance covers the goods on board; freight insurance covers the freight the shipping company would lose if the goods are lost and do not reach the destination.
Insurable interest: life – at the time of the contract; fire – both at the contract and at the time of loss; marine – at the time of loss.

Indemnity: not applicable to life; applicable to fire and marine. Duration: life is long-term; fire is usually for one year; marine is for a voyage or a period. Surrender value: only life insurance policies have a surrender value.

ex.q: A shipping company fears that if a vessel sinks, it will not be paid its freight charges. Which marine insurance should it buy?
st: The risk is the loss of freight income, not of the ship or goods.
That is covered by freight insurance.
ex.a: Freight insurance.

topics.rl: Exporters shipping from Kandla or Nhava Sheva usually buy cargo insurance so that goods lost at sea are compensated.

rv.summary: Fire insurance covers accidental fire loss with indemnity; marine insurance covers hull, cargo and freight. Life, fire and marine differ in when insurable interest is needed, indemnity, duration and surrender value.
focus: Elements of fire insurance, especially accidental fire
Hull vs cargo vs freight insurance
Comparing life, fire and marine on insurable interest, indemnity, duration and surrender value
remember: Insurable interest: life – at contract; fire – at contract and at loss; marine – at loss
Hull: ship; cargo: goods; freight: freight income
Only life policies have a surrender value
traps: Deliberate fire is not covered by fire insurance
Don't mix up cargo (goods) and freight (shipping charges) insurance
A fire policy is usually for one year, not for life

topics.h: India Post has one of the largest postal networks in the world, reaching villages where no bank branch exists. It does far more than deliver letters.
p: Financial facilities: savings schemes such as the Public Provident Fund (PPF), Kisan Vikas Patra, National Savings Certificate, recurring deposit and monthly income scheme; money orders to transfer money.

Mail facilities: parcel (transmission of articles from one place to another); registered post (safe delivery, with proof of posting and delivery); insured post (for valuable articles; the post office compensates loss or damage in transit up to the insured value).

Allied facilities: greetings post (greeting cards), media post (brands can advertise on postcards, letters and post boxes), direct post (direct advertising material delivered to targeted homes), international money transfer, passport facilities, speed post (fast, time-bound delivery), e-bill post (collecting bill payments), and courier services.
Project idea: visit a nearby post office or bank, note the services offered and how customers use them, and present your findings.
Note: this course follows the CBSE 2026-27 syllabus, so the transport, warehousing and telecom parts of the printed book are not covered.

ex.q: Farida wants to send her gold earrings by post to her sister and be compensated if they are lost. Which postal service should she use?
st: Valuable articles need cover for loss in transit.
Insured post compensates up to the insured value.
ex.a: Insured post.

topics.rl: The India Post Payments Bank and post office savings schemes bring banking to remote villages through the postman's doorstep services.

rv.summary: India Post offers financial facilities (savings schemes, money orders), mail facilities (parcel, registered and insured post) and allied facilities such as speed post, media post, direct post, greetings post and e-bill post.

Registered post vs insured post
Media post vs direct post

Mail: parcel, registered post, insured post
Allied: greetings, media, direct, speed, e-bill post, passports, courier
traps: Registered post gives proof of delivery but does not compensate valuables; insured post does
Speed post is allied, not a financial facility
Media post advertises on postal stationery; direct post sends ads to targeted homes

topics.t: Digitisation and the meaning of e-business
topics.h: A saree weaver in Pochampally can now sell to a buyer in Toronto without leaving her village. Technology has changed not just what business sells, but how business is done.
p: Business is being digitised: activities such as buying, selling, ordering, payments, record-keeping and communication are increasingly done through computers, the internet and mobile networks.
E-business means carrying out industry, trade and commerce using computer networks. It covers all business transactions and functions conducted electronically.
E-commerce covers a firm's interactions with its customers and suppliers over the internet, i.e. mainly buying and selling online.

E-business is wider than e-commerce: besides online buying and selling, it includes internal functions such as production, inventory management, product development, accounting, finance and human resource management done electronically.

ex.q: A company sells shoes on its website, and also uses an online system to track factory output and pay salaries. Which parts are e-commerce and which are e-business?
st: Online sale of shoes to customers = e-commerce (buying and selling).
Tracking production and paying salaries online = internal functions, part of e-business.
E-business includes e-commerce plus such internal activities.
ex.a: Selling online is e-commerce; the whole set, including production tracking and payroll, is e-business.

topics.rl: Government e-Marketplace (GeM) lets government departments buy from sellers online, and GSTN lets businesses file returns online: business and its paperwork are going digital.

rv.summary: E-business means carrying out industry, trade and commerce using computer networks. It is wider than e-commerce, which covers only online buying and selling with customers and suppliers.
focus: The meaning of digitisation and e-business
Telling e-business from e-commerce
Classifying an activity as internal (e-business only) or buying and selling (e-commerce)
remember: E-business = e-commerce + internal functions (production, inventory, accounting, finance, HR) done electronically
E-commerce: a firm's online dealings with customers and suppliers
traps: E-commerce is a part of e-business, not wider than it
Online HR or production tracking is e-business, not e-commerce
E-business is more than just selling on a website

topics.t: Scope of e-business: B2B, B2C, intra-B and C2C
topics.h: When a carmaker orders tyres online, when you buy a T-shirt on an app, when HR emails your offer letter and when you sell your old cycle on a resale site, four different kinds of e-business are at work.
p: B2B (business-to-business): transactions between firms, e.g. a manufacturer ordering components from suppliers online, or dealing with distributors and dealers electronically. It helps keep inventory low and speeds up procurement.
B2C (business-to-customers): firms selling to consumers online, plus marketing, after-sales support and feedback. Customers can order any time, and firms can track preferences.
Intra-B (within business): interactions within the firm, e.g. linking departments, employees and plants through networks; it supports flexible manufacturing and coordination.
C2C (consumer-to-consumer): consumers selling to other consumers through online platforms, e.g. second-hand books, furniture or clothes; the platform provides the marketplace.

ex.q: Classify: (a) a bakery chain orders flour online from a mill; (b) a student sells her old calculator to another student on a resale app; (c) a company's sales and production departments share orders on its intranet.
st: (a) Two businesses transacting = B2B.
(b) One consumer selling to another = C2C.
(c) Within the same company = intra-B.
ex.a: (a) B2B, (b) C2C, (c) intra-B.

topics.rl: Indian resale platforms for used cars and gadgets are C2C, online grocery apps are B2C, and B2B platforms let kirana stores restock from distributors.

topics.h: A traditional shop needs a building, a location near customers and staff at the counter. An online shop needs a good website and a delivery partner. The differences run deep.
p: Ease of formation: e-business is easy; traditional business is relatively difficult. Physical presence: not required vs required. Location: no locational requirement vs proximity to raw materials or markets needed.
Cost of setting up and operating: low for e-business (no need for physical premises) vs high for traditional business (rent, staff, inventory).
Nature of contact with suppliers and customers: direct in e-business vs often through intermediaries in traditional business. Internal communication: non-hierarchical (direct, fast) vs hierarchical.

Response time: instantaneous vs long. Business processes are simplified in e-business. Opportunity for inter-personal touch and physical pre-sampling of products: less in e-business, more in traditional business.

Ease of global reach: more in e-business. Government support: much (e-business is promoted under IT policies). Transaction risk: high in e-business (distance and anonymity) vs low in traditional business.

ex.q: A customer wants to touch and try a lehenga before buying. Which kind of business suits her, and on which basis?
st: She wants to see and feel the product before purchase.
Physical pre-sampling is easier in a traditional store.
On the basis of 'opportunity for physical pre-sampling', traditional business scores higher.
ex.a: Traditional business, on the basis of physical pre-sampling and inter-personal touch.

topics.rl: Many Indian brands that started online (selling eyewear, mattresses or clothes) later opened physical stores, because some customers want to try products in person.

topics.h: A teenager in Indore can launch an online T-shirt store with a laptop and a small budget, and get her first order from Kerala the same night.
p: Ease of formation and lower investment requirements: an e-business can be set up quickly with relatively little capital, compared with a physical business.
Convenience: the internet allows business 24 × 7, so customers can shop and firms can operate at any time. This is often called 24 × 7 access.
Speed: buying, selling, information exchange and payments take place much faster; digital products like software and e-books can even be delivered instantly.
Global reach and access: an online firm can reach buyers and suppliers anywhere in the world, so the market is truly global.
Movement towards a paperless society: e-business reduces dependence on paper for orders, invoices and records, e.g. online returns, e-tickets and digital receipts.

ex.q: Neeraj, a chess coach in Jaipur, starts selling recorded lessons online. Within a month he has students in Dubai and the USA and receives payments at night. Which benefits does this show?
st: Students abroad = global reach.
Payments at night = convenience of 24 × 7 access.

topics.h: You can order a phone in ten seconds, but it may take three days to arrive, and you can't shake the seller's hand. E-business has its weak spots too.
p: Low personal touch: online dealings lack the warmth and trust of face-to-face interaction, so they suit standardised goods better than goods needing personal attention, like tailored clothes.
Incongruence between order taking and delivery speed: information and orders move instantly, but physical goods still take time to deliver.
Need for technology skills: e-business requires the ability to use IT on the part of all parties.

ex.a: Incongruence between order taking and delivery speed.

topics.rl: Many elderly people in India still prefer the local chemist over online pharmacies, showing low personal touch and resistance as real limits of e-business.

topics.h: From searching 'running shoes' to the doorbell ringing with your parcel, every online purchase follows the same three stages.
p: Pre-purchase/sale stage: the buyer searches for information about products and sellers; to buy, he usually registers on the website with name, address, contact details and a password, creating an account.
Ordering stage: the buyer selects items into a virtual 'shopping cart' and, once satisfied, places the order and chooses a payment method.
Delivery stage: physical goods are delivered through couriers or delivery partners; digital goods (e-books, software, music) can be delivered instantly online.

Payment mechanisms: cash on delivery (COD) (payment in cash when goods arrive); cheque (sent to the seller, goods dispatched after it clears); net banking transfer (buyer transfers money through internet banking); credit and debit cards (card details are entered and the amount is charged); digital cash (electronic money held in a bank account or wallet and used for online payment).

ex.q: Arrange the steps of an online purchase: place order, register on the site, receive delivery, add items to cart.
st: First register on the site (pre-purchase).
Then add items to the shopping cart.
Then place the order and pay.
Finally receive the delivery.
ex.a: Register → add to cart → place order → receive delivery.

topics.rl: Cash on delivery remains popular in many Indian towns because buyers like to see the parcel before paying.

topics.t: Security and safety of e-transactions; resources needed
topics.h: A fake shopping site, a stolen card number, a virus wiping customer records: online business is only as strong as its security.
p: Transaction risks: default on order taking or giving (seller denies receiving an order, or buyer denies placing it); default on delivery (goods not delivered, delivered late or wrong goods sent); default on payment (seller not paid, or buyer pays but does not get the goods).
Data storage and transmission risks: viruses can damage stored data; hackers may break into systems and steal or alter data while it is stored or transmitted.
Risk of threat to intellectual property and privacy: once information is online, it can be copied or misused, and personal data of customers may be exposed.

Safeguards: encryption (converting data into a code that only authorised parties can read), secure payment gateways, strong passwords and authentication such as OTPs, firewalls and antivirus software, and reliable sellers' policies.

Resources for a successful e-business: a well-developed website; technically competent staff; adequate computer hardware, software and network infrastructure; and efficient payment and delivery systems.

ex.q: An online shop's customer database is stolen by someone who breaks into its server. Which risk is this, and which safeguard would have helped?
st: Unauthorised access to stored data is hacking, a data storage and transmission risk.
Encrypting stored data and using firewalls would have protected it.
ex.a: Data storage risk (hacking); encryption and firewalls would help.

topics.rl: Indian banks send OTPs for online card payments: a two-step authentication that makes e-transactions safer.

topics.ch: Social Responsibilities of Business and Business Ethics
topics.h: A company may follow every law and still pollute a river right up to the legal limit. Is that enough? Social responsibility asks business to do more than the law demands.
p: Social responsibility of business is its obligation to make decisions and take actions that are desirable in terms of the objectives and values of society.

Legal responsibility means obeying laws: it is compulsory and enforced by the state. Social responsibility is broader and largely voluntary: it includes legal duties plus actions that benefit society beyond what the law requires.
A socially responsible business looks at the effect of its decisions on owners, workers, consumers, the government, the community and the environment, not just on profit.

In India, Section 135 of the Companies Act, 2013 requires certain large companies to spend a part of their profits on Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) activities, making some social spending a legal duty for them.

ex.q: A cement company pays its taxes, follows pollution norms and also, on its own, runs a free school and plants trees near its plant. Which actions are legal responsibility and which go beyond it?
st: Paying taxes and following pollution norms are required by law: legal responsibility.
Running a free school and planting trees are voluntary actions that benefit society beyond the law.
Social responsibility includes both, but is wider than legal responsibility.
ex.a: Taxes and pollution norms: legal responsibility; free school and tree planting: social responsibility beyond the law.

topics.rl: Many Indian companies run CSR projects in sanitation, education and health in villages around their plants.

topics.ch: Social Responsibilities of Business and Business Ethics
topics.h: Why should a profit-making company care about the village next to its factory? Because, in the long run, its own survival depends on it.
p: Justification for existence and growth: business exists to serve society; its long-run growth depends on providing goods and services that society values.

Long-term interest of the firm: a good public image built through social responsibility helps the firm in the long run. Avoidance of government regulation: voluntary responsible behaviour reduces the need for strict government rules.

Maintenance of society: if business ignores society, people may react with protests; responsible behaviour helps maintain peace and order. Availability of resources with business: business has finance and talent that can be used to solve social problems.

Converting problems into opportunities: business can turn social problems into profitable opportunities (e.g. cleaner technology, waste recycling). Better environment for doing business: a society with fewer problems gives better conditions for business.
Holding business responsible for social problems: business has often caused or added to problems like pollution, so it should help solve them.

ex.q: A paper mill that polluted a river now treats its waste water and also sells recycled paper made from waste. Which arguments for social responsibility does this reflect?
st: The mill contributed to pollution, so it takes responsibility for the problem.
Selling recycled paper turns a waste problem into a business opportunity.
ex.a: Holding business responsible for social problems, and converting problems into opportunities.

topics.rl: Some Indian companies have turned waste plastic into roads and furniture: converting a social problem into a business opportunity.

topics.ch: Social Responsibilities of Business and Business Ethics
topics.t: The case against social responsibility, and the reality
topics.h: Some economists argue that a business does its job best by maximising profit and leaving social work to the government. Do they have a point?
p: Violation of profit-maximisation objective: critics say the only responsibility of business is to maximise profits; SR goes against this.
Burden on consumers: the cost of social programmes may be passed on to consumers through higher prices.
Lack of social skills: business managers are trained in business, not in solving social problems, which should be left to specialised agencies.
Lack of broad public support: the public generally does not like business getting involved in social programmes, so it is hard to run them successfully.

Reality: forces that have made business more socially responsive include threat of public regulation, pressure of labour movement, impact of consumer consciousness, development of social standards, development of business education, the link between social interest and business interest, and development of a professional managerial class.

ex.q: A critic says: 'A toy maker spending on village schools will raise toy prices and its managers know nothing about teaching.' Which two arguments against SR is he making?
st: Higher prices passed to buyers = burden on consumers.
Managers lacking expertise in education = lack of social skills.
ex.a: Burden on consumers and lack of social skills.

topics.rl: Growing consumer awareness in India, through consumer forums and social media reviews, pushes firms to act more responsibly.

topics.ch: Social Responsibilities of Business and Business Ethics
topics.h: Making good products, obeying the law, not hurting religious sentiments in ads and donating to flood relief: four very different kinds of responsibility.
p: Economic responsibility: as an economic institution, business must produce goods and services that society wants and sell them at a profit.
Legal responsibility: every business must obey the laws of the land; a law-abiding firm is a socially responsible one.
Ethical responsibility: behaviour that society expects but which is not written into law, e.g. respecting religious sentiments and dignity of people while advertising.
Discretionary responsibility: purely voluntary obligations that a firm takes on, e.g. donating to charity, supporting educational institutions or helping flood victims.

In case questions, look for clues: 'produce what society wants at a profit' → economic; 'comply with law' → legal; 'not required by law, but expected' → ethical; 'voluntary donation or charity' → discretionary.

ex.q: A detergent company withdraws an ad that could hurt a community's religious feelings, though no law required this. Which kind of responsibility is this?
st: No law required it, so it is not legal responsibility.
It is behaviour society expects, respecting sentiments.
That is ethical responsibility.
ex.a: Ethical responsibility.

topics.rl: During floods in Assam and Kerala, many companies donated relief material and money on their own: discretionary responsibility.

topics.ch: Social Responsibilities of Business and Business Ethics
topics.h: Shareholders want returns, workers want fair pay, customers want quality and the town wants clean air. A responsible business balances all of them.
p: Towards shareholders/owners: provide a fair and regular return on investment; ensure safety of investment; give regular, accurate and full information about the company's working.
Towards workers: provide opportunity for meaningful work; good working conditions; fair wages; democratic leadership; respect for workers' right to form unions; welfare facilities.

Towards consumers: supply goods of the right quality at reasonable prices; avoid adulteration, poor quality and misleading or dishonest advertising; provide after-sales service; inform consumers about the product; ensure safety.
Towards the government and community: respect the law and pay taxes honestly; behave as a good citizen; protect the natural environment; help weaker and backward sections; respect social values.

ex.q: A company (a) declares a fair dividend, (b) installs safety guards on machines, (c) stops adding cheap filler to its spices, and (d) pays taxes honestly. Match each to the interest group.
st: (a) Dividend = responsibility to shareholders.
(b) Machine safety = responsibility to workers.
(c) No adulteration = responsibility to consumers.
(d) Honest taxes = responsibility to the government.
ex.a: (a) Shareholders, (b) workers, (c) consumers, (d) government.

topics.rl: Consumer commissions under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 hear complaints when firms fail in their responsibility towards consumers.

rv.summary: A business has responsibilities to shareholders (fair return, safety, information), workers (fair wages, safe conditions, unions, welfare), consumers (quality, fair price, honesty, after-sales) and government and community (laws, taxes, environment).

topics.ch: Social Responsibilities of Business and Business Ethics
topics.h: The smog over north Indian cities every winter and foam on some rivers are reminders that business activity can harm the environment.
p: Environment means the totality of man's surroundings, both natural and man-made. Pollution is the addition of harmful substances that damage it.

Causes of pollution by business: air pollution (smoke and gases from factories and vehicles, e.g. carbon monoxide); water pollution (chemicals and waste dumped into rivers and lakes); land pollution (dumping of toxic and industrial waste on land, reducing its quality); noise pollution (factories and vehicles, causing stress, hearing problems and other health issues).

Need for pollution control: reduction of health hazards; reduced risk of liability (firms may have to pay damages to victims); cost savings (efficient processes cut waste); improved public image; other social benefits (clearer visibility, cleaner buildings, better quality of life and natural resources).

Role of business: definite commitment by top management; ensuring the commitment is shared by all employees; clear policies for good raw materials, clean technology and scientific waste disposal; complying with laws; participating in government programmes (e.g. cleaning rivers, tree plantation); periodic assessment of pollution control programmes; educational workshops and training.

ex.q: A dyeing unit in Tiruppur discharges coloured waste water into a river. Name the type of pollution, one health or legal risk to the firm, and one step it can take.
st: Waste into a river = water pollution.
Risk: health hazards for people downstream and liability to pay damages.
Step: install effluent treatment and adopt cleaner technology.
ex.a: Water pollution; health hazard and liability risk; treat effluent and use clean technology.

topics.rl: Under the Namami Gange programme, industries along the Ganga are required to treat their waste water, and many businesses take part in cleanup drives.

rv.summary: Business causes air, water, land and noise pollution. Controlling it reduces health hazards and liability, saves costs and improves image. Business can help through top management commitment, clean technology, compliance and training.

topics.ch: Social Responsibilities of Business and Business Ethics
topics.h: A salesman could earn a bigger bonus by hiding a product defect. Nothing stops him except ethics.
p: Business ethics refers to the socially determined moral principles and standards that should govern business activities; they guide what is right and wrong in business conduct.
Ethics and social responsibility are linked: ethical behaviour (honesty, fairness, not cheating) is the base of responsible business.

Elements of business ethics: top management commitment (leaders must set the example); publication of a 'code' (a written code of ethics covering fundamental honesty, adherence to laws, product safety and quality, workplace health and safety, conflicts of interest, employment practices, marketing practices, financial reporting, etc.).

Establishment of compliance mechanisms (e.g. careful recruitment, training, reporting systems for violations, audits); involving employees at all levels (employees at every level implement ethics, so they must be involved); measuring results (regularly checking how well ethical standards are followed).

ex.q: A company prints a code of conduct, but its CEO regularly ignores it, and no one checks whether it is followed. Which elements of business ethics are missing?
st: The CEO ignoring the code = no top management commitment.
No checking = no compliance mechanism and no measuring of results.
A code alone is not enough.
ex.a: Top management commitment, compliance mechanisms and measuring results are missing.

topics.t: Business finance and classification of sources
topics.h: Before a single machine runs or a single shirt is sold, a business needs money. Where it gets that money from shapes its risk, control and cost.
p: Business finance means the funds required for carrying out business activities. Fixed capital requirements are funds for fixed assets (land, building, machinery); working capital requirements are funds for day-to-day operations (raw materials, wages, rent).

By period: long-term sources (more than 5 years), e.g. equity shares, preference shares, debentures, long-term loans from financial institutions; medium-term (more than 1 year but less than 5 years), e.g. bank loans, public deposits, lease financing; short-term (less than 1 year), e.g. trade credit, short-term bank loans, commercial paper.

By ownership: owners' funds (provided by the owners, e.g. equity shares and retained earnings; permanent, no fixed return, owners get control) vs borrowed funds (raised as loans, e.g. debentures, bank loans, public deposits, trade credit; for a fixed period, fixed interest, often secured by assets, no control to lenders).

By source of generation: internal sources (generated within the business, e.g. retained earnings, collection of receivables, disposing of surplus inventory) vs external sources (raised from outside, e.g. shares, debentures, loans, trade credit, public deposits).

ex.q: Classify retained earnings on all three bases: period, ownership and source of generation.
st: Period: it is a permanent, long-term source.
Ownership: profits belong to the owners, so it is owners' funds.
Generation: it comes from within the business, so it is internal.
ex.a: Long-term, owners' funds, internal source.

topics.rl: A Tiruppur garment exporter may buy machines using a long-term bank loan but pay for yarn using 60 days' trade credit from the mill: matching finance with need.

topics.h: When you buy one share of a listed company, you become a part-owner. You may vote at its meetings, and you get what is left after everyone else is paid.
p: Equity shares are the most important source of raising long-term capital. Equity shareholders are the owners of the company; equity is also called 'ownership capital' or 'owners' funds'. They bear the highest risk.

Rights: voting rights (they elect directors and decide policies); right to a share in residual income and assets (paid after preference shareholders and creditors); pre-emptive right (to be offered new shares first, as 'right shares').

Merits: suitable for investors willing to take risk for higher returns; no burden on the company to pay a fixed dividend; permanent capital, repayable only on winding up; provides credibility and a base for borrowing; no charge on assets; democratic control through voting.

Limitations: investors who want steady income may not prefer them; cost of equity is higher (dividends are not tax-deductible, and issue costs are high); issue of more equity can dilute voting power of existing shareholders; more formalities and delays.

ex.q: A company has a profit of ₹10,00,000 to distribute. It must first pay ₹2,00,000 as preference dividend. It has 1,00,000 equity shares. If the whole remainder is distributed, what is the dividend per equity share?
st: Dividend per share = 8,00,000 ÷ 1,00,000 = ₹8.
ex.a: ₹8 per equity share.

topics.h: Preference shareholders are like passengers with priority boarding: they get their dividend and their capital back before equity shareholders, but they usually cannot steer the plane.
p: Preference shares carry two preferential rights over equity shares: (i) to receive a fixed rate of dividend out of profits before equity holders, and (ii) to receive repayment of capital before equity holders on winding up. They generally have no voting rights except on matters affecting their own rights.

Merits: steady income for investors who want safety; no dilution of control; no charge on assets; fixed dividend lets equity holders earn more when profits are high (trading on equity); preference in liquidation.

Limitations: not suitable for investors willing to take risk; reduces equity holders' claims on assets; rate of dividend is usually higher than debenture interest; dividend is not tax-deductible, so they are costlier than debt.

Types: cumulative (unpaid dividend accumulates and is paid in later profitable years) vs non-cumulative (arrears lapse); participating (share in surplus profits after equity dividend) vs non-participating; convertible (can be converted into equity) vs non-convertible.
Equity vs preference: dividend fluctuating vs fixed; paid last vs before equity; full voting vs limited voting; higher risk vs lower risk; capital repaid last vs before equity.

ex.q: A company has ₹5,00,000 of 10% cumulative preference shares. It paid no dividend for two years. In year 3, it has enough profit. How much preference dividend must it pay before any equity dividend?
st: Annual dividend = 10% of 5,00,000 = ₹50,000.
Arrears for 2 years = ₹1,00,000, plus ₹50,000 for year 3.

topics.rl: Some Indian banks and companies issue preference shares to raise capital without giving up voting control.

topics.h: Instead of paying out all its profit, a company can keep some of it to buy new machines. Money it doesn't have to borrow or beg for: retained earnings.
p: A company does not distribute all its profits as dividend; it keeps a part for future use. This is called retained earnings or ploughing back of profits. It is an internal source of finance, a part of owners' funds.

Merits: permanent source of funds; no explicit cost in the form of interest, dividend or issue expenses; no dilution of control; enhances the company's capacity to absorb unexpected losses; may lead to an increase in the market price of equity shares.

Limitations: excessive ploughing back may cause dissatisfaction among shareholders, as they get lower dividends; it is an uncertain source, since profits fluctuate; the opportunity cost of these funds is often not recognised, which may lead to their sub-optimal use.

ex.q: A company earns a net profit of ₹50,00,000 and pays 40% of it as dividend. How much is ploughed back?
ex.a: ₹30,00,000 is retained.

topics.rl: Many large Indian companies fund new plants largely from their own reserves, built up by years of ploughing back profits.

topics.h: If a company sells you a '9% debenture', you are not an owner but a lender. You get 9% interest every year, profit or loss.
p: Debentures (and bonds) are instruments for raising long-term debt capital. A debenture is an acknowledgement of debt by the company; debenture holders are creditors who get a fixed rate of interest, e.g. 9% debentures pay 9% interest every year on their face value.

Merits: preferred by investors who want fixed income at lesser risk; fixed charge, so holders do not share in extra profits; no dilution of control (no voting rights); interest is a tax-deductible expense, so debt is cheaper than shares.
Limitations: fixed obligation to pay interest is a burden in lean years; the company must provide for redemption; assets may be mortgaged, reducing further borrowing capacity.

Types: secured (charge on assets) vs unsecured; registered (names recorded, transfer by a regular instrument) vs bearer (transferable by delivery); convertible (into equity) vs non-convertible; first (repaid before second) vs second debentures.

Shares vs debentures: ownership capital vs borrowed capital; holders are owners vs creditors; dividend (paid only from profits) vs interest (paid even if there is a loss); voting rights vs no voting rights; no security vs usually secured; repaid after creditors vs repaid before shareholders on winding up.

ex.q: A company issues 20,000 10% debentures of ₹100 each. What is the annual interest? If it is in the 30% tax bracket, how much tax does this interest save?
st: Interest is tax-deductible: tax saved = 30% of 2,00,000 = ₹60,000.
ex.a: Interest ₹2,00,000 a year; tax saved ₹60,000.

topics.rl: Large Indian companies such as power and infrastructure firms often raise funds through non-convertible debentures listed on stock exchanges.

topics.t: Loans from commercial banks and financial institutions
topics.h: A small firm needs ₹10 lakh for three years for new machines; a big firm needs ₹500 crore for fifteen years for a new plant. They usually knock on different doors.
p: Commercial banks give loans for fixed periods, cash credit, overdrafts and other facilities, usually for short and medium terms, and generally against security.

Merits of bank loans: timely financial assistance; secrecy is maintained (no public disclosure needed); an easier source as no prospectus or issue formalities are needed; flexible, since the loan can be increased or repaid early.

Limitations of bank loans: generally for short periods, and extension or renewal is uncertain; detailed investigation and securities or personal guarantees are needed; banks may impose restrictive terms, e.g. on sale of mortgaged goods.

Financial institutions (such as IFCI, the State Financial Corporations and, historically, ICICI and IDBI) were set up by the central and state governments to give long and medium-term finance, especially for expansion and modernisation.

Merits of FI loans: long-term finance not available from banks; financial, managerial and technical advice; loan obtained increases goodwill; easy instalment repayment; available even during depression. Limitations: rigid criteria and lengthy formalities; restrictions on dividend payments; FIs may nominate directors to the board, restricting management freedom.

ex.q: A company takes a ₹12,00,000 term loan at 10% simple interest per year, repayable at the end of 3 years. How much interest does it pay in total?
st: Interest per year = 10% of 12,00,000 = ₹1,20,000.

topics.rl: State Financial Corporations in many states have long funded small and medium industries for setting up and expanding plants.

rv.summary: Commercial banks give short and medium-term loans with secrecy and flexibility, but need security and renewal is uncertain. Financial institutions give long-term finance and advice, but have rigid terms and may nominate directors.

topics.h: A kirana store picks up ₹50,000 of goods today and pays the wholesaler after 30 days. That is a loan, without any bank involved.
p: Trade credit is the credit extended by one trader to another when goods are bought on credit without immediate payment. It appears in the buyer's books as sundry creditors or accounts payable. It is a short-term source of finance.

Merits of trade credit: a convenient and continuous source; readily available if the buyer's creditworthiness is known; promotes sales by letting buyers stock more; does not create any charge on assets.
Limitations of trade credit: easy credit may induce overtrading and add to risks; only a limited amount is available; generally costly compared with most other sources (cash discounts are lost).

Inter-corporate deposits (ICDs) are unsecured short-term deposits made by one company with another. Types: three months deposits, six months deposits, and call deposits (withdrawable by the lender on giving one day's notice).

Characteristics of ICDs: the rate of interest varies with the amount, period and creditworthiness; the ICD market is unorganised, informal and based on mutual trust; they are mainly used to meet short-term cash shortages.

ex.q: A retailer buys goods worth ₹1,00,000 on 60 days' credit. The supplier offers a 2% cash discount for immediate payment. What does the retailer give up by using trade credit?

By taking 60 days' credit, the retailer loses this discount.
This lost discount is the cost of trade credit.
ex.a: He gives up a ₹2,000 cash discount.

topics.rl: Textile traders in Surat and Ludhiana run much of their business on trade credit, built on years of trust between buyers and sellers.

rv.summary: Trade credit is short-term credit given by suppliers on goods bought; it is convenient but limited and costly through lost discounts. ICDs are unsecured short-term deposits between companies in an informal market.

topics.t: Other sources: factoring, lease financing, public deposits and commercial paper
topics.h: A company can rent a machine instead of buying it, sell its unpaid bills to collect cash early, or borrow from the public for a few years. Finance has many doors.
p: Factoring: a financial service in which a factor (often a bank subsidiary) buys a firm's receivables or collects them on its behalf, and may also provide credit information. Merits: cheaper than financing receivables through other sources; quick cash; no charge on assets; the firm can focus on its business. Limitations: may be costly when invoices are many and small; the factor may pressurise customers, hurting goodwill.

Lease financing: the lessor (owner) gives the lessee the right to use an asset in return for periodic lease rentals. Merits: assets can be acquired with lower investment; simple documentation; lease rentals are tax-deductible; no dilution of ownership; lessor bears the risk of obsolescence. Limitations: restrictions on use; operations may suffer if the lease is not renewed; may be costlier than buying; the lessee does not become the owner.

Public deposits: deposits raised by companies directly from the public, usually at higher interest than bank deposits, generally for medium terms. Merits: simple procedure; cost lower than bank loans; no charge on assets; no dilution of control. Limitations: new companies find it hard to raise; unreliable when large amounts are needed; collection may be difficult.

Commercial paper (CP): an unsecured promissory note issued by a firm to raise short-term funds (up to one year). Merits: sold directly to investors, no restrictive conditions; freely transferable; provides more funds than many sources; a continuous source since a maturing CP can be repaid by a fresh issue; companies can park surplus funds in CP. Limitations: only financially sound, highly rated firms can issue it; amount limited by the surplus liquidity of investors; it is an impersonal method and maturity cannot be extended.
Note: discounting of bills of exchange and international sources (ADR, GDR) were removed in rationalisation and are not covered.

ex.q: A logistics firm wants 50 trucks but does not want to block ₹20 crore in buying them. It pays monthly rentals to a finance company that owns the trucks. Which source is this, and who bears obsolescence risk?
st: Using an asset owned by another in return for rent = lease financing.
The finance company is the lessor; the logistics firm is the lessee.
The lessor bears the risk of obsolescence.
ex.a: Lease financing; the lessor bears obsolescence risk.

topics.rl: Many Indian airlines lease most of their aircraft instead of buying them, saving huge capital outlay.

topics.t: Factors affecting the choice of source of funds
topics.h: Equity, debentures, bank loan, trade credit... there is no single 'best' source. The right one depends on cost, risk, control, time and more.
p: Cost: both the cost of procurement (issue expenses) and the cost of using the funds (interest, dividend) matter. Financial strength and stability of operations: a firm with stable earnings can take on fixed-charge debt; an unstable one should prefer owners' funds.

Form of organisation and legal status: a sole trader or partnership cannot issue shares; companies can. Purpose and time period: long-term needs (fixed assets) should be met by long-term sources; short-term needs (working capital) by short-term sources.

Risk profile: equity is the least risky for the company (no fixed obligation); debt is riskier (fixed interest and repayment). Control: issuing equity can dilute control; debt and preference shares do not.

Effect on creditworthiness: heavy secured debt may reduce the firm's ability to borrow further and its credit standing. Flexibility and ease: restrictive conditions of some lenders reduce flexibility.
Tax benefits: interest on debentures and loans is tax-deductible, while dividends on shares are not, so debt is tax-efficient.

ex.q: The founders of a company want to raise ₹10 crore for expansion without losing control. Profits are stable. Which source suits them, and on which factors?

Stable profits mean they can bear fixed interest.
Interest is tax-deductible.
So debentures or a long-term loan suit them.
ex.a: Debentures or long-term loans, based on control, financial stability and tax benefit.

topics.rl: Many family-controlled Indian groups prefer borrowing over issuing new shares to avoid diluting promoters' control.

topics.t: MSMEs: meaning, classification and Udyam registration
topics.h: From a pickle unit in Andhra to a CNC machine shop in Rajkot to a small software firm in Kochi, crores of Indians work in micro, small and medium enterprises.
p: MSME stands for Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises. The Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development (MSMED) Act, 2006 classifies enterprises as manufacturing enterprises (producing goods) and service enterprises (providing services).
The Act originally used investment in plant and machinery (for manufacturing) or in equipment (for services) to classify units, with separate limits for each.

Under the revised criteria notified by the government, classification uses a composite test: investment in plant and machinery or equipment AND annual turnover. The same limits now apply to manufacturing and service enterprises. The exact limits are revised from time to time by government notification. For example, the limits in force from 1 April 2025 are: micro – investment up to ₹2.5 crore and turnover up to ₹10 crore; small – up to ₹25 crore and ₹100 crore; medium – up to ₹125 crore and ₹500 crore. (From July 2020 to March 2025 they were ₹1 crore/₹5 crore, ₹10 crore/₹50 crore and ₹50 crore/₹250 crore.)
An enterprise is classified as micro, small or medium according to which band its investment and turnover both fall within; exceeding either limit moves it to the next category.

Udyam Registration: MSMEs register online on the Udyam portal, free of cost, on the basis of self-declaration using Aadhaar. The registration helps them access government schemes, priority-sector loans and other benefits.

ex.q: A small machine shop's investment fits within the 'small' limit, but its turnover crosses the 'small' turnover limit. How will it be classified under the composite criteria?
st: Both investment and turnover must be within a category's limits.
Turnover exceeds the small-enterprise limit.
So it moves to the next category, medium (if within medium limits).
ex.a: It will be classified as a medium enterprise (assuming it is within the medium limits).

topics.rl: Udyam registration has made it easier for small units across India to register online and become eligible for schemes and easier bank credit.

rv.summary: MSMEs are classified as manufacturing or service enterprises under the MSMED Act, 2006. Under the composite criteria, both investment and turnover must fall within a band, with the same limits for both types. Registration is free on the Udyam portal.

topics.t: Role of small business in India and in rural India
topics.h: Small businesses are the second-largest employer in India after agriculture. They make everything from matchboxes to machine parts.
p: Role in India: small businesses are the largest source of employment after agriculture; they produce a wide variety of products, from mass consumer goods to sophisticated items; they contribute significantly to industrial output, exports and GDP.

They promote balanced regional development by setting up in rural and backward areas; use local resources and skills; offer opportunities for entrepreneurship; have low cost of production; and allow quick and timely decision making and personalised relations with customers and employees.
Role in rural India: cottage and village industries provide non-farm employment and income to rural people, especially in agricultural off-seasons.
This curbs migration of rural people to cities, reduces poverty and income inequality, and helps develop village industries using local skills, such as handloom, pottery and handicrafts.

ex.q: A village near Moradabad has many brassware artisans working from home. How does this industry help the village?
st: It gives non-farm employment and income to villagers.
People do not need to migrate to cities for work.
It uses local skills and helps reduce rural poverty.
ex.a: Non-farm employment, curbs migration, uses local skills and reduces poverty.

topics.rl: Khadi and village industries, handloom clusters and food-processing units in villages show how small businesses keep rural economies alive.

rv.summary: Small businesses are India's largest employer after agriculture and add to output, exports and balanced regional growth. In rural India, cottage and village industries give non-farm jobs, curb migration and reduce poverty.

topics.h: A talented craftsman in Channapatna makes beautiful wooden toys, yet struggles to get a bank loan, buy wood in bulk or sell beyond his town. Small businesses face many hurdles.
p: Finance: difficulty in getting adequate credit due to lack of collateral and credit history; working-capital shortage due to delayed payments by buyers.
Raw materials: difficulty in getting good-quality raw materials at reasonable prices because they buy in small quantities and have low bargaining power.
Managerial skills: the owner may lack knowledge of all areas such as finance, marketing and HR. Marketing: weak marketing; dependence on middlemen who may exploit them.

Quality: many units cannot afford quality testing and standards. Capacity utilisation: lack of marketing and demand leads to under-use of capacity, raising costs. Technology: outdated technology leads to low productivity.

Sickness: internal causes (lack of skilled labour and managerial skills) and external causes (delayed payments, shortage of working capital, inadequate loans) can make units sick. Global competition: since liberalisation, small units face competition from large and multinational firms.

ex.q: A small unit sells parts to a big company that pays after 120 days. The unit cannot pay wages on time and stops production. Which problems are shown?
st: Late payment by the buyer creates a shortage of working capital (finance).
Inability to continue production is a sign of sickness due to an external cause.
ex.a: Finance (working-capital shortage due to delayed payments) leading to sickness.

topics.rl: To tackle delayed payments, the government set up online platforms like TReDS where MSMEs can get early payment on their bills from large buyers.

topics.t: Government support: NSIC and District Industries Centres
topics.h: A first-time entrepreneur in a small district town doesn't know where to begin. Government bodies like NSIC and the District Industries Centre exist precisely for her.
p: The National Small Industries Corporation (NSIC) was set up in 1955 to promote, aid and foster the growth of small businesses in the country.

NSIC support: supplying indigenous and imported machines on easy hire-purchase terms; procuring, supplying and distributing raw materials; helping small units export and develop export-worthiness; mentoring and advisory services; acting as technology business incubator; creating awareness of technology upgradation; developing software technology parks and technology transfer centres; marketing support.
District Industries Centres (DICs) were launched on 1 May 1978 to provide an integrated administrative framework at the district level for promoting small, tiny, village and cottage industries.

DICs act as a single-window agency at the district level: they help identify viable projects and entrepreneurs, arrange finance, machinery and raw materials, and provide marketing, training and other support under one roof.

ex.q: Sunita in Bhilwara wants to start a small textile unit but needs help to find a viable project, arrange a loan and get machines. Where should she go first?
st: She needs many services at the local level, under one roof.
The District Industries Centre is the single-window agency at the district level.
ex.a: The District Industries Centre (DIC) of her district.

topics.h: Every big company you know, from a two-wheeler giant to a food-delivery app, began with one person spotting an opportunity and daring to act.
p: Entrepreneur: the person who sets up a business enterprise, taking the risk to start it. Entrepreneurship: the process of setting up one's own business, as distinct from pursuing a profession or employment. Enterprise: the business organisation that is created through this process.
Systematic activity: entrepreneurship requires knowledge, skills and competencies that can be learnt and developed; it is not just luck or inborn talent.
Lawful and purposeful activity: the activity must be within the law, and its purpose is to create value for the entrepreneur and society.
Innovation: entrepreneurs create new products, processes or markets, or find new ways of doing things; this creates value.

Organisation of production: the entrepreneur brings together land, labour, capital and technology to produce goods and services. Risk-taking: the entrepreneur bears the risk of failure, but takes moderate, calculated risks.

ex.q: Asha leaves her bank job and starts 'Asha's Millet Snacks'. Identify the entrepreneur, the entrepreneurship and the enterprise.

The process of setting up her own business: entrepreneurship.
The business created: Asha's Millet Snacks, the enterprise.

topics.rl: Many Indian founders started small, in garages or college hostels, showing that entrepreneurship is a learnable, systematic activity.

topics.t: Need for entrepreneurship and the entrepreneurial process
topics.h: India needs crores of new jobs every decade. Government offices and big companies alone cannot create them; entrepreneurs can.
p: Need for entrepreneurship in economic development: it raises production and GDP; encourages capital formation by mobilising savings; generates employment for the entrepreneur and others; creates business opportunities for suppliers and other firms; improves economic efficiency through innovation; increases the scope of economic activities; benefits local communities; and fosters a spirit of exploration and adventure.

There is no single fixed list of stages; one common way to describe the journey of starting a venture is: (1) identify a business opportunity or idea; (2) evaluate it through feasibility study and market research; (3) prepare a business plan; (4) mobilise resources such as finance, people, technology and premises; (5) launch the enterprise and manage it; (6) grow and expand.
Ideas often come from problems people face, changes in technology, new trends and gaps in existing markets.
A business plan describes the product, target market, competitors, operations, team and financial projections; it guides the founder and convinces investors and lenders.
In the CBSE syllabus, the process of entrepreneurship development is studied mainly through the Startup India scheme and the ways to fund start-ups (next topic).

ex.q: Rahul notices that people in his town have no affordable bicycle repair service. He surveys demand, writes a plan, borrows money, opens a shop and later opens two more. Map his steps to the process.
st: Notices the gap: identify opportunity.
Surveys demand: evaluate the idea.
Writes a plan: business plan.
Borrows money and sets up: mobilise resources and launch.
Opens two more: growth.
ex.a: Opportunity → evaluation → business plan → resources → launch → growth.

topics.rl: Incubation centres at IITs, IIMs and many universities help students move from idea to business plan to launch.

rv.summary: Entrepreneurship drives development by raising output, mobilising savings, creating jobs and opportunities and improving efficiency. A common process is: identify opportunity, evaluate it, write a business plan, mobilise resources, launch and grow.

topics.t: Startup India and ways to fund start-ups
topics.h: In 2016 India launched Startup India. Today the country has one of the largest startup ecosystems in the world. How do these ventures get their first rupee?
p: Startup India was launched by the Government of India on 16 January 2016 to build a strong ecosystem for innovation and start-ups, drive economic growth and create jobs.

Its action plan focuses on three areas: simplification and handholding (easier compliance, self-certification, a single online hub); funding support and incentives (a Fund of Funds, credit guarantees, tax benefits for recognised start-ups); and industry-academia partnership and incubation (incubators, research parks, innovation challenges).

Bootstrapping: funding the venture with the founder's own savings and early revenues, keeping costs low. Crowdfunding: raising small amounts from a large number of people, usually through online platforms.

Angel investment: wealthy individuals invest their own money in early-stage start-ups in exchange for equity, often adding mentoring. Venture capital: professionally managed funds invest in high-growth start-ups for equity, along with guidance, usually at a later stage than angels.

Business incubators and accelerators: incubators nurture very early-stage ideas with space, mentoring and networks over a longer period; accelerators run short, intensive programmes to speed up the growth of existing start-ups. Microfinance and NBFCs: small loans to entrepreneurs who lack access to regular banking.

ex.q: Arrange a typical funding journey of a tech start-up: venture capital, bootstrapping, angel investment.
st: The founder first uses own savings: bootstrapping.
Then an individual investor puts in early money: angel investment.
Later a professional fund invests for growth: venture capital.
ex.a: Bootstrapping → angel investment → venture capital.

topics.rl: Startup India's portal lets founders apply for recognition online, and many state governments run their own startup policies and incubators.

rv.summary: Startup India (16 January 2016) supports start-ups through simplification, funding and incubation. Start-ups are funded through bootstrapping, crowdfunding, angel investors, venture capital, incubators and accelerators, and microfinance.

topics.h: Your brand name, your app's code, your invention and even the region your tea comes from can all be protected by law. Ideas are property too.
p: Intellectual property refers to creations of the mind: inventions, literary and artistic works, designs, symbols, names and images used in business. Intellectual property rights (IPR) are legal rights that protect these creations and give the creator exclusive rights to use them for a period.

Copyright: protects literary, dramatic, musical and artistic works, cinematograph films, sound recordings and computer software. Trademark: a word, name, symbol, logo or design that distinguishes the goods or services of one firm from others (registration is valid for 10 years and renewable).

Patent: an exclusive right granted for an invention that is new, involves an inventive step and is capable of industrial application; in India, a patent lasts 20 years. Design: protects the new or original shape, configuration, pattern or ornamentation applied to an article (its visual appearance).

Geographical indication (GI): identifies goods as originating from a specific place, where a quality or reputation is linked to that origin, e.g. Darjeeling tea, Banarasi sarees, Kanchipuram silk. Plant variety: protects new plant varieties developed by breeders and farmers. Semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design: protects the layout of transistors and circuit elements on chips.
Why start-ups need IPR: to prevent copying of their innovation, build brand value, attract investors, earn through licensing, and gain a competitive edge.

ex.q: A start-up (a) invents a new water-purifying filter, (b) names it 'PuriDrop' with a logo, and (c) writes the software for its app. Which IPR protects each?
st: New invention with industrial application = patent.
Brand name and logo = trademark.
Computer software = copyright.
ex.a: (a) Patent, (b) trademark, (c) copyright.

topics.rl: Darjeeling tea was India's first product to get a geographical indication tag, so only tea grown in that region can be sold under the name.

rv.summary: Intellectual property rights protect creations of the mind. Types include copyright, trademark, patent (20 years in India), design, geographical indication, plant variety and semiconductor layout-design. Start-ups use IPR to stop copying and build value.

topics.h: Biscuits made in a factory near Pune reach a tiny shop in Arunachal. In between stands a quiet hero of trade: the wholesaler.
p: Internal trade is the buying and selling of goods and services within the boundaries of a nation. No customs duty or import duty is levied, since goods are produced and sold within the country. It is classified into wholesale trade and retail trade.
Wholesale trade means buying and selling goods in large quantities, usually from manufacturers, and selling them to retailers or other businesses (not to final consumers).

Services of wholesalers to manufacturers: facilitating large-scale production (by buying in bulk); bearing risk (of price fall, theft, spoilage); financial assistance (paying cash for goods, sometimes in advance); expert advice (on consumer preferences and market trends); help in marketing (distributing to many retailers); facilitating continuity of production; storage (warehousing goods until needed).

Services of wholesalers to retailers: availability of goods (ready stock from many producers); marketing support (advertising and promotion); grant of credit; specialised knowledge (about products and demand); risk sharing (retailers buy in small lots, so they carry less stock).

ex.q: A wholesaler buys 10,000 packets of tea from a manufacturer each month, stores them and sells to 200 small shops on 15 days' credit. Name one service to the manufacturer and one to the retailers.
st: Buying in bulk and storing goods helps the manufacturer produce on a large scale continuously.
Selling on 15 days' credit helps retailers: grant of credit.
ex.a: To manufacturer: facilitating large-scale production and storage; to retailers: grant of credit.

topics.rl: Wholesale mandis like Azadpur in Delhi and Vashi in Navi Mumbai move huge volumes of fruits and vegetables from farmers to thousands of retailers every day.

rv.summary: Internal trade is buying and selling within a country, with no customs duty, and is wholesale or retail. Wholesalers buy in bulk from manufacturers and sell to retailers, serving both with finance, storage, risk bearing, credit and information.

topics.t: Retail trade and services of retailers
topics.h: The corner kirana shop knows your family's favourite brand of atta, offers credit until the month-end and introduces new products. It is the final link to the consumer.
p: A retailer is a business enterprise that sells goods and services directly to final consumers for their personal, non-business use, usually in small quantities. Retailing is the last link in the chain of distribution.

Services to manufacturers and wholesalers: help in distribution (making goods available to scattered consumers); personal selling (explaining and persuading); enabling large-scale operations (so producers and wholesalers need not deal with each consumer); collecting market information (about tastes and preferences); help in promotion (displays and in-store promotion).

Services to consumers: regular availability of products; new products information; convenience in buying (small quantities, near homes, long hours); wide selection; after-sales services (delivery, repairs, spare parts); credit facilities to regular buyers.

ex.q: A mobile shop owner tells the company that young buyers in his area prefer phones with big batteries. Which service of retailers is this?
st: He is passing on information about customer preferences to the company.
That is collecting market information.
ex.a: Collecting market information (a service to manufacturers).

topics.rl: Kirana stores in India often deliver groceries home and offer monthly credit to regular customers: classic retailer services.

rv.summary: A retailer sells goods directly to final consumers in small quantities and is the last link in distribution. Retailers serve producers (distribution, selling, market information, promotion) and consumers (availability, information, convenience, choice, after-sales, credit).

topics.h: The vegetable vendor with a handcart, the weekly haat in a village, the man selling toys outside a railway station: retailers who come to you.
p: Itinerant retailers are traders who do not have a fixed place of business; they keep moving from place to place in search of customers. They deal in consumer goods of daily use, often of low value, and give time and place utility.
Peddlers and hawkers: carry goods on bicycles, handcarts, cycle-rickshaws or on their heads, and sell from place to place at the doorstep of customers, e.g. vegetables, fruits, snacks, toys.
Market traders: open shops at different places on fixed days or dates, e.g. weekly markets (haats) on Mondays in one place and Thursdays in another.

Street traders (pavement vendors): sell at places with huge floating population, such as near railway stations, bus stands and busy streets; they sell common-use items like stationery, eatables, newspapers and readymade garments.

Cheap jacks: have independent shops of a temporary nature in a business locality; they keep changing their location depending on the potential of the place, and deal in consumer items and repairs (e.g. watches, shoes, buckets).

ex.q: Ramu sets up a temporary stall near a new housing colony to repair shoes and sell buckets. After three months he shifts to another locality with better business. What type of itinerant retailer is he?
st: He has a temporary shop, not just a moving cart.
He shifts location according to business potential.
That describes a cheap jack.
ex.a: Cheap jack.

topics.rl: Weekly haats in tribal areas of Chhattisgarh and Jharkhand are run by market traders who visit different villages on fixed days.

rv.summary: Itinerant retailers have no fixed place of business and sell low-value daily goods. Types: peddlers and hawkers (door to door), market traders (fixed days), street traders (busy places) and cheap jacks (temporary shops that shift).

topics.h: The general store in your colony, the school-uniform shop near the bus stop and the second-hand bookshop near college: all are fixed-shop small retailers.
p: Fixed-shop retailers have permanent establishments to sell their goods; they have greater resources than itinerant retailers and offer more services like home delivery and credit.
General stores: located in residential areas, they stock a variety of products for daily needs, such as groceries, toiletries and stationery, and are open for long hours.
Speciality shops: sell a specific type of product within a line, e.g. only children's garments, men's wear, school uniforms or college books; they are usually in central locations.
Single line stores: sell a single product line but in a wide variety, e.g. readymade garments, watches, shoes, books, computers.

Street stall holders: small vendors at street crossings or busy places, selling cheap goods like hosiery, toys, soft drinks; they have a small fixed stall. Second-hand goods shops: sell used goods such as books, clothes, furniture and utensils at lower prices.

ex.q: Classify: (a) a shop selling only school uniforms; (b) a shop selling all kinds of footwear; (c) a shop selling old furniture.
st: (a) A specific type within the clothing line: speciality shop.
(b) One line (footwear) in many varieties: single line store.
(c) Used goods: second-hand goods shop.
ex.a: (a) Speciality shop, (b) single line store, (c) second-hand goods shop.

topics.rl: Old Delhi's Daryaganj book market and many college-town shops sell second-hand books at a fraction of the price.

rv.summary: Fixed-shop small retailers have permanent shops and more services. Types: general stores, speciality shops, single line stores, street stall holders and second-hand goods shops.

topics.h: Clothes on the first floor, electronics on the second, a café on the third, all under one roof. That is the departmental store.
p: A departmental store is a large establishment offering a wide variety of products, classified into well-defined departments, aimed at satisfying practically every need of the customer under one roof. Each department specialises in one line.

Features: large size, usually centrally located; provides facilities like restaurants, travel bureaus, rest rooms and parking under one roof; combines retailing with warehousing; buys directly from manufacturers; centralised purchasing and decentralised sales across departments; often organised as a company with a board.

Merits: attracts a large number of customers due to central location; convenience in buying (all needs under one roof); attractive services; economy of large-scale operations; promotion of sales through advertising and display.

Limitations: lack of personal attention to customers; high operating cost (rent, staff, services), so prices tend to be high; high possibility of losses due to high costs and changing demand; inconvenient location for buyers who need something urgently, since it is usually in the city centre.

ex.q: Mrs Iyer wants to buy a saree, a pressure cooker and a toy, and have lunch, without travelling to different shops. Which retail format suits her, and which merit does this show?
st: She needs many types of goods plus food in one place.
A departmental store has many departments and services under one roof.
This shows the merit of convenience in buying.
ex.a: Departmental store; merit: convenience in buying.

topics.rl: Large multi-department stores in Indian city malls, with fashion, home and beauty sections under one roof, follow the departmental store model.

rv.summary: A departmental store is a large, centrally located store with many departments under one roof. It offers convenience and services and large-scale economies, but has high costs and prices, little personal attention and an inconvenient location for urgent needs.
