topics.t: Chain stores (multiple shops) and comparison with departmental stores
topics.h: The same shoe shop with the same look, same prices and same products in Pune, Patna and Puducherry: that is a chain store.
p: Chain stores or multiple shops are networks of retail shops owned and operated by manufacturers or intermediaries, located in different localities across the country, with similar appearance and dealing in standardised, branded products.

Features: located in fairly populous localities; manufacturing or purchasing is centralised at the head office; each shop is supervised by a branch manager; the head office controls policies; prices are fixed and all sales are on a cash basis; sales proceeds are deposited daily; dealing in a limited range of products.

Merits: economies of scale (central purchasing); elimination of middlemen; no bad debts (cash sales); transfer of goods from one branch to another; diffusion of risk (losses in one shop offset by profits in others); low cost of operation; flexibility (an unprofitable shop can be closed or shifted).

Limitations: limited selection of goods (only the firm's own range); lack of initiative (branch managers follow head office instructions); lack of personal touch; difficult to change products quickly when demand changes.

Departmental store vs chain store: one central location vs many localities near customers; wide variety of products vs limited range of a specific type; maximum services vs limited services; prices not uniform (discounts used to clear stock) vs uniform fixed prices; may give credit vs strictly cash; caters mostly to higher-income groups vs various income groups.

ex.q: A shoe company has 400 shops across India. One shop in a small town keeps making losses. What can the company do, and which merits of chain stores does this show?
st: It can close or shift the loss-making shop: flexibility.
Profits of the other shops cover this loss: diffusion of risk.
It can also move unsold stock to branches with higher demand.
ex.a: Close or shift the shop and move stock; shows flexibility, diffusion of risk and transfer of goods.

topics.rl: Footwear, pharmacy and fashion chains with identical-looking outlets across Indian towns are classic multiple shops.

rv.summary: Chain stores are networks of similar shops in many localities, run by a head office, selling standardised goods at fixed prices for cash. They enjoy scale, no bad debts and spread risk, but offer limited choice and little initiative.

topics.h: Long before apps, people in small towns ordered books, seeds and gadgets from catalogues and received them by post. That is mail order business.
p: Mail order houses are retail outlets that sell goods through mail. There is generally no direct personal contact between buyers and sellers.

Prospective customers are approached through advertisements in newspapers and magazines, circulars, catalogues, samples and price lists sent by post. Orders are received by mail, and goods are sent through the post office, often by VPP (value payable post), where the customer pays on delivery.
Suitable for: standardised and graded goods, which can be easily described; goods that can be transported easily at low cost; not suitable for perishable goods or goods requiring personal inspection.

Merits: limited capital requirement (no costly shop); elimination of middlemen; absence of bad debts (payment in advance or on delivery); wide reach (anywhere the post reaches); convenience (goods delivered at the doorstep).

Limitations: lack of personal contact; high promotion costs (advertising and catalogues); no after-sales services; no facility of credit; possibility of abuse (fraud by dishonest sellers); dependence on postal services.

ex.q: A firm in Delhi sells standard-size calendars and diaries through catalogues sent by post and delivers them by VPP. Why are bad debts absent?
st: Under VPP, the customer pays when the parcel is delivered.
The post office collects the money before handing over goods.
No goods are given on credit.
ex.a: Because payment is collected on delivery (VPP), so there is no credit and hence no bad debts.

topics.rl: India Post's value payable post service made mail order business possible across small towns, and today's e-commerce is its digital descendant.

rv.summary: Mail order houses sell by post without personal contact, reaching buyers through ads and catalogues and delivering by VPP. They suit standardised, easily transported goods, need little capital and have no bad debts, but offer no credit or after-sales service.

topics.t: Goods and Services Tax (GST): concept and structure
topics.h: Before 2017, goods crossing state borders faced different taxes and long queues of trucks at check posts. GST changed this with 'One Nation, One Tax'.
p: Goods and Services Tax (GST) is a comprehensive, destination-based indirect tax levied on the supply of goods and services. It came into force on 1 July 2017 after the Constitution (101st Amendment) Act, 2016.

It replaced many central and state indirect taxes, such as central excise duty, service tax, VAT, central sales tax, entry tax, octroi and luxury tax. Destination-based means the tax revenue goes to the state where goods or services are consumed.

Intra-state supply (within the same state): Central GST (CGST) and State GST (SGST) are levied, shared equally; in Union Territories without their own legislature, UTGST replaces SGST. Example: at 18%, it is CGST 9% + SGST 9%.
Inter-state supply (from one state to another) and imports: Integrated GST (IGST) is levied by the Centre, and later shared with the destination state. Example: at 18%, IGST is 18%.
The GST Council, chaired by the Union Finance Minister and including state finance ministers, recommends GST rates, exemptions and rules.

ex.q: A trader in Jaipur sells goods worth ₹50,000 at 18% GST (a) to a buyer in Jodhpur and (b) to a buyer in Pune. What taxes apply in each case?
st: (a) Jaipur to Jodhpur is within Rajasthan: intra-state.
(b) Jaipur to Pune is from Rajasthan to Maharashtra: inter-state.

topics.rl: After GST, many state-border check posts were removed, cutting the time trucks spend waiting on highways.

rv.summary: GST is a destination-based indirect tax on the supply of goods and services, in force from 1 July 2017. Intra-state supply attracts CGST + SGST (equal halves); inter-state supply and imports attract IGST. The GST Council recommends rates.

topics.t: Input tax credit, GSTN, composition scheme and chambers of commerce
topics.h: Before GST, a shopkeeper often paid tax on tax: the tax already included in his purchase price was taxed again when he sold. Input tax credit fixed this.
p: Input tax credit (ITC): a registered business can deduct the GST it has already paid on purchases (input tax) from the GST it collects on sales (output tax), and pays only the difference. This removes the cascading effect (tax on tax).
GSTN (Goods and Services Tax Network) is the IT backbone of GST: it provides the online portal for registration, filing returns and paying tax for taxpayers, the Centre and states.

Registration: businesses whose aggregate turnover crosses a prescribed threshold must register. At present the threshold is ₹40 lakh a year for most suppliers of goods and ₹20 lakh for service providers, with lower limits in some special-category states; the government can revise it.

Composition scheme: an optional, simpler scheme for small taxpayers (turnover up to ₹1.5 crore for most traders and manufacturers), who pay tax at a low fixed rate on their turnover with fewer returns; they cannot claim input tax credit and cannot charge GST to their customers on their bills.

Chambers of commerce and industry, such as FICCI, CII and ASSOCHAM, promote internal trade by working with government on transportation and inter-state movement, harmonisation of taxes and levies, marketing of agro-products, weights and measures and prevention of duplicate brands, promoting sound infrastructure, and simplifying labour laws.

ex.q: A manufacturer sells goods to a retailer for ₹10,000 + 18% GST. The retailer sells them for ₹15,000 + 18% GST. How much GST does the retailer pay to the government after input tax credit?
st: Input tax (paid on purchase) = 18% of 10,000 = ₹1,800.
Output tax (collected on sale) = 18% of 15,000 = ₹2,700.
Net GST payable = 2,700 − 1,800 = ₹900.
This equals 18% of the value added (₹5,000).

topics.rl: Every month lakhs of businesses file their GST returns online on the GST portal run by GSTN.

rv.summary: Input tax credit lets a business deduct GST paid on purchases from GST collected on sales, removing tax on tax. GSTN runs the GST portal. Small taxpayers may choose the composition scheme. Chambers of commerce promote internal trade.

topics.h: Indian software runs banks in London, Gulf oil fuels Indian cars, and Japanese technology makes Indian metro coaches. No country is an island in business.
p: International business refers to manufacturing and trade beyond national boundaries. It includes not only cross-border trade in goods and services, but also the movement of capital, personnel, technology and intellectual property (patents, trademarks, know-how and copyrights).

International trade means exports and imports of goods and services. International business is wider: it covers trade plus foreign investment, licensing, franchising and other forms of cross-border operations.

Main reason: countries cannot produce everything equally well or cheaply, because of unequal distribution of natural resources (e.g. oil in the Gulf, iron ore in some countries) and differences in labour productivity and production costs.
So each country specialises in what it can produce more efficiently and trades for the rest. This specialisation benefits all trading nations.

ex.q: India imports crude oil but exports IT services. Explain why, using the reasons for international business.
st: India does not have enough crude oil reserves: unequal distribution of natural resources.
India has a large pool of skilled, cost-effective IT professionals: differences in labour productivity and costs.
So India specialises in IT services and trades for oil.
ex.a: Due to unequal natural resources and differences in labour productivity and costs, India specialises in IT and imports oil.

topics.rl: Indian generic medicines are exported to many countries because India can produce them at lower cost: specialisation in action.

rv.summary: International business is manufacturing and trade beyond national borders, including movement of capital, people, technology and intellectual property. It arises because resources, productivity and costs differ, so countries specialise and trade.

topics.t: Domestic vs international business; scope of international business
topics.h: Selling sarees in Jaipur and selling sarees in Japan both involve sarees, but the currency, laws, customers and risks are completely different.
p: Differences between domestic and international business: nationality of buyers and sellers (same vs different countries); nationality of other stakeholders (employees, suppliers, investors); mobility of factors of production (free within a country, restricted across countries); customer heterogeneity (different tastes, languages, cultures); differences in business systems and practices; political systems and risks; business regulations and policies (tariffs, quotas, standards); currency (one currency vs different currencies and exchange-rate changes).

Scope: merchandise exports and imports (tangible goods); service exports and imports, also called invisible trade (tourism and travel, transportation, business services such as banking, insurance, software).
Licensing and franchising: permitting a firm in another country to use patents, trademarks, technical know-how or a business model in return for a fee (royalty).

Foreign investment: foreign direct investment (FDI) means investing directly in plants, machinery or a controlling stake abroad, with control over management; portfolio investment means buying shares or giving loans abroad to earn dividends or interest, without control.

ex.q: A US fund buys 2% shares of an Indian listed company only to earn dividends, while a Korean carmaker builds and runs a factory in Tamil Nadu. Classify both investments.
st: Buying a small stake for dividends, without control = portfolio investment.
Building and running a factory with management control = FDI.
ex.a: US fund: portfolio investment; Korean carmaker: FDI.

topics.rl: Foreign tourists visiting Rajasthan and spending money in India count as service exports for India, even though no goods leave the country.

rv.summary: International business differs from domestic business in nationality of parties, factor mobility, customer variety, business systems, politics, regulations and currency. Its scope covers merchandise and service trade, licensing and franchising, and foreign investment.

topics.h: When an Indian pharma company sells medicines in Africa, India earns dollars, the company earns more profit, and workers in its plants get more jobs. Everyone wins.
p: Benefits to nations: earning foreign exchange, which helps pay for imports of capital goods, technology and oil.

More efficient use of resources (each country produces what it is good at); improving growth prospects and employment potential; increased standard of living through access to a wider variety of goods and services.
Benefits to firms: prospects for higher profits (when prices abroad are higher); increased capacity utilisation (using surplus capacity by selling abroad).
Prospects for growth (when domestic demand is saturated); a way out of intense competition in the domestic market; improved business vision (thinking globally makes firms more competitive).

ex.q: A tractor maker uses only 60% of its plant capacity because home demand is low. It starts exporting to Africa and uses 90%. Which benefit to firms is this?
st: Capacity used rises from 60% to 90%.
This is increased capacity utilisation, which also reduces cost per unit.
ex.a: Increased capacity utilisation.

topics.rl: India's large IT and pharma exports earn foreign exchange that helps pay for crude oil and electronics imports.

rv.summary: International business benefits nations through foreign exchange, efficient use of resources, growth and jobs and a higher standard of living. It benefits firms through higher profits, capacity use, growth, escape from home competition and better vision.

topics.t: Modes of entry: exporting/importing and contract manufacturing
topics.h: A firm can enter a foreign market by just shipping goods there, or by getting a local factory to make its products. These are the two simplest doors to global business.
p: Exporting means sending goods and services from the home country to a foreign country; importing means buying them from abroad. Direct exporting/importing: the firm itself approaches overseas buyers or suppliers and handles all formalities. Indirect: the firm works through intermediaries such as export houses or buying offices of foreign customers.
Merits of exporting/importing: the easiest way to enter international markets; less involvement and less investment (no need to set up units abroad); less risk compared with other modes.

Limitations: added costs of packaging, transportation and insurance make goods costlier abroad; not possible where the importing country has restrictions; exporters operate from home and have little direct contact with foreign markets.

Contract manufacturing (outsourcing): a firm enters into a contract with local manufacturers in foreign countries to produce certain components or goods as per its specifications. Merits: large-scale production without investing in facilities; little investment risk; cost advantage (local labour and materials); local producers get business.

Limitations of contract manufacturing: local firms may not follow quality standards; the local manufacturer loses control over the manufacturing process, since goods are made strictly as per the contract; the local firm cannot sell the goods freely and must sell to the international firm at predetermined prices.

ex.q: A European clothing brand gets an Indian factory in Tiruppur to make T-shirts with its designs and labels, and buys all of them at an agreed price. Which mode of entry is this, and one limitation for the Indian factory?
st: Production by a local firm as per the foreign firm's specifications = contract manufacturing.
The Indian factory must sell to the brand at predetermined prices and cannot sell the T-shirts freely.
ex.a: Contract manufacturing; the local firm cannot sell freely and gets predetermined prices.

topics.rl: Many global brands get their garments, phones and toys made by contract manufacturers in India.

rv.summary: Exporting and importing is the simplest, lowest-investment entry mode, direct or indirect, but adds costs. Contract manufacturing gets goods made by local foreign firms to specification, saving investment, but quality may slip and local firms must sell at fixed prices.

Exporting is the least risky, not the riskiest, mode

topics.t: Modes of entry: licensing, franchising, joint ventures and wholly owned subsidiaries
topics.h: A burger chain's outlet in Delhi, a car plant owned jointly by Indian and foreign firms, and a foreign company's 100%-owned Indian unit: three deeper ways to go global.
p: Licensing: a firm (licensor) permits a foreign firm (licensee) to use its patents, trademarks, copyrights or technical know-how for a fee called royalty. Franchising is similar but is generally used for services; the franchiser gives a business model and exercises stricter control over the franchisee. Merits: less expensive and low risk for the licensor (licensee invests); licensor does not bear losses; low risk of government takeover as local owners run the business; licensee's local knowledge helps. Limitations: licensee may later become a competitor; trade secrets may leak; conflicts over accounts, royalty and quality.

Joint venture (JV): a firm jointly owned by two or more independent firms. It can be formed when a foreign firm buys an interest in a local firm, a local firm buys an interest in a foreign firm, or both jointly form a new enterprise. Merits: less financial burden for the foreign firm; large projects become possible; benefit of the local partner's knowledge of markets, culture and politics; risks are shared. Limitations: technology and trade secrets may be revealed to the partner; dual ownership can cause conflicts.

Wholly owned subsidiary (WOS): the parent company acquires full control (100% equity) over a foreign company, either by setting up a new firm (greenfield venture) or by acquiring an established firm. Merits: full control over operations; no need to share technology or trade secrets. Limitations: 100% investment, so not suitable for small and medium firms; the parent bears all losses; some countries are averse to full foreign ownership, raising political risk.
Comparing modes: exporting and licensing need the least investment abroad; a joint venture needs more; a wholly owned subsidiary needs the most investment and gives the most control.

ex.q: A foreign pizza brand lets an Indian company run outlets under its name, menu and systems, and checks quality strictly in return for fees. Which mode is this, and how does it differ from licensing?
st: Use of brand plus a full business system in services, with strict control = franchising.
Licensing is mainly for production and marketing of goods using patents or know-how, with less control.
Franchising is mainly for services, with stricter control by the franchiser.
ex.a: Franchising; it applies to services with stricter control, while licensing applies to goods.

topics.rl: Many international fast-food and coffee chains operate in India through franchise partners, while some automobile companies run 100% subsidiaries.

rv.summary: Licensing and franchising let foreign firms use patents, brands or a business model for royalty. A joint venture shares ownership with a local firm. A wholly owned subsidiary gives 100% control but needs full investment and risk.

Franchising: services, stricter control
WOS: 100% equity, via greenfield venture or acquisition

topics.t: Export procedure (I): from enquiry to production
topics.h: A buyer in Dubai emails an Indian carpet maker in Bhadohi asking for prices. Seventeen steps later, the carpets are on a ship and the money is in the bank.
p: Step 1, receipt of enquiry and sending quotations: the importer asks about prices, quality and terms; the exporter replies with a quotation, often in the form of a proforma invoice (giving details of quality, grade, size, weight, price and terms of export).
Step 2, receipt of order or indent: if the importer accepts, he places an order or indent describing the goods, price, quantity, packing and delivery terms.

Step 3, assessing the importer's creditworthiness and securing a guarantee for payment: the exporter usually asks for a letter of credit, a guarantee issued by the importer's bank that it will honour payment up to a certain amount.

Step 4, obtaining an export licence: the exporter must get an Importer Exporter Code (IEC) number from the Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT), and register with the appropriate Export Promotion Council (getting a Registration-cum-Membership Certificate, RCMC); registration with the Export Credit Guarantee Corporation (ECGC) protects against payment risks.
Step 5, obtaining pre-shipment finance from a bank to buy raw materials, process and pack goods; Step 6, production or procurement of goods as per the importer's specifications.

ex.q: Put these early export steps in order: obtain IEC number, receive order, send proforma invoice, get letter of credit.
st: First reply to the enquiry with a proforma invoice (quotation).
Then receive the order or indent.
Then secure payment guarantee: letter of credit.
Then obtain the export licence, including the IEC number.
ex.a: Send proforma invoice → receive order → get letter of credit → obtain IEC number.

topics.rl: The DGFT issues IEC numbers online; without one, an Indian business cannot legally export or import.

rv.summary: The export procedure begins with enquiry and proforma invoice, receipt of order (indent), checking creditworthiness with a letter of credit, getting the IEC from DGFT and RCMC, obtaining pre-shipment finance and producing the goods.
focus: The order of the early export steps
Meaning of proforma invoice, indent and letter of credit
IEC (DGFT), RCMC and ECGC
remember: Proforma invoice: exporter's quotation
Indent: importer's order
LC: importer's bank's payment guarantee
IEC from DGFT; RCMC from Export Promotion Council
traps: The indent comes from the importer, not the exporter
Pre-shipment finance comes before production, not after shipping
The IEC is issued by DGFT, not the RBI

topics.t: Export procedure (II): from inspection to payment
topics.h: The carpets are ready. Now come inspection, customs, the ship's receipt, the bill of lading and finally the payment.
p: Step 7, shipment inspection: for certain goods, inspection by the Export Inspection Agency (EIA) or another authorised body is compulsory, and a certificate of inspection is issued. Step 8, excise clearance: the book lists this step, in which the exporter applies to the excise authorities for clearance of excise duty on the goods; such duty on exports was generally exempted or refunded, and since 2017 GST has replaced central excise on most goods, with exports treated as zero-rated. Step 9, obtaining a certificate of origin, which shows the country where goods are made, so the importer may claim tariff concessions.

Step 10, reservation of shipping space: the exporter applies to the shipping company; it issues a shipping order, an instruction to the captain of the ship to receive the specified goods on board. Step 11, packing and forwarding: goods are properly packed and marked and sent to the port. Step 12, insurance of goods against risks at sea.

Step 13, customs clearance: the exporter prepares a shipping bill, the main document on the basis of which customs gives permission to export. Step 14, obtaining mate's receipt: after loading, the captain (mate) of the ship issues a mate's receipt to the exporter, acknowledging receipt of the cargo on board.

Step 15, payment of freight and issue of bill of lading: on paying freight, the shipping company issues a bill of lading, which is evidence that it has accepted the goods for carriage and is a document of title (an airway bill is used for air cargo). Step 16, preparation of invoice, stating quantity and the amount payable.

Step 17, securing payment: the exporter sends the shipping documents through his bank to the importer's bank, along with a bill of exchange. Under a sight draft, documents are released on payment (D/P); under a usance draft, documents are released on acceptance of the bill (D/A), and payment is made later.

ex.q: Arrange: bill of lading, shipping bill, mate's receipt, shipping order.
st: Book space: the shipping company issues the shipping order.
Customs clearance needs the shipping bill.
After loading, the captain issues the mate's receipt.
On paying freight, the shipping company issues the bill of lading.
ex.a: Shipping order → shipping bill → mate's receipt → bill of lading.

topics.rl: Exporters from ports such as Nhava Sheva and Chennai file shipping bills electronically through the customs system before cargo is loaded.

rv.summary: Later export steps: inspection, excise clearance, certificate of origin, shipping order, packing, insurance, customs clearance with shipping bill, mate's receipt, bill of lading, invoice and securing payment through sight (D/P) or usance (D/A) drafts.

topics.h: A Ludhiana firm wants machines from Germany. It must find a supplier, get permission, arrange foreign currency, pay and clear customs before the machines reach its factory.
p: Step 1, trade enquiry: the importer collects information about exporters and their terms, and asks for quotations (often receiving a proforma invoice). Step 2, procurement of import licence: the importer checks the EXIM policy to see if a licence is needed, and must have an IEC number from the DGFT.

Step 3, obtaining foreign exchange: the importer applies to a bank authorised by the RBI for foreign exchange, as per foreign exchange regulations. Step 4, placing order or indent with the exporter. Step 5, obtaining a letter of credit from his bank in favour of the exporter, if agreed.

Step 6, arranging finance to pay for the goods on arrival. Step 7, receipt of shipment advice from the exporter, giving details such as invoice number, bill of lading number, name of vessel, port and date of shipment.

Step 8, retirement of import documents: the importer pays (sight draft) or accepts the bill of exchange (usance draft) to get the shipping documents, such as the bill of lading, from the bank. Step 9, arrival of goods at the port.

Step 10, customs clearance and release of goods: the importer gets a delivery order from the shipping company, pays the dock dues (getting a port trust dues receipt), fills in a bill of entry (giving details of goods for customs and assessment of import duty), gets the goods examined and pays the import duty; the goods are then released.

ex.q: An importer pays the bank the amount of a sight draft and collects the bill of lading. Which step of the import procedure is this?
st: Taking up shipping documents from the bank by paying or accepting the bill of exchange is called retirement of import documents.
ex.a: Retirement of import documents.

topics.rl: A project idea: interview a local importer or exporter, or study one firm's documents, and draw a flow chart of its import or export procedure.

rv.summary: Import procedure: trade enquiry, import licence and IEC, foreign exchange from an RBI-authorised bank, placing the order, letter of credit, arranging finance, shipment advice, retirement of documents, arrival of goods and customs clearance with a bill of entry.

Retirement of import documents
Customs clearance: delivery order, dock dues, bill of entry, import duty
remember: Bill of entry: import customs document for assessing duty
Retirement: paying or accepting the bill to get shipping documents
Foreign exchange from an RBI-authorised bank
traps: The bill of entry is for imports, not exports
Shipment advice is sent by the exporter, not the importer
Trade enquiry, not customs clearance, is the first step

topics.h: International trade runs on paper (or PDFs): one document orders, another guarantees payment, another proves the goods are on the ship. Mix them up and the cargo gets stuck.
p: Indent: an order placed by the importer with the exporter for supply of goods. Proforma invoice: a quotation giving details of quality, grade, size, weight, price and terms.

Letter of credit (LC): a guarantee by the importer's bank that it will honour payment up to a certain amount on presentation of specified documents. Certificate of origin: shows the country of manufacture.
Shipping order: issued by the shipping company to the ship's captain to receive the specified goods on board. Shipping bill: the main document for customs permission to export.

Mate's receipt: issued by the captain after the cargo is loaded. Bill of lading: issued by the shipping company accepting goods for carriage by sea; a document of title. Airway bill: the equivalent document for goods sent by air.

Bill of exchange: a written instrument in which the exporter (drawer) orders the importer (drawee) to pay a certain sum to a specified person. Sight draft: payable on presentation (documents released against payment). Usance draft: payable after a specified period (documents released against acceptance).

ex.q: Which document would you use if the goods are sent by air instead of by sea, in place of the bill of lading?
st: The bill of lading is for sea transport.
For air cargo, the airline issues an airway bill.
ex.a: Airway bill.

topics.rl: Under the government's trade facilitation drive, many Indian trade documents are now filed and verified electronically, cutting delays at ports.

rv.summary: Key trade documents: indent, proforma invoice, letter of credit, certificate of origin, shipping order, shipping bill, mate's receipt, bill of lading (sea) or airway bill (air), and bill of exchange as sight or usance draft.

Bill of lading vs airway bill
Sight vs usance draft; drawer vs drawee

Bill of exchange: exporter (drawer) orders importer (drawee) to pay
Sight: on presentation; usance: after a period

A letter of credit is issued by the importer's bank, not the shipping company
The indent is not a quotation

topics.h: Which body sets rules so that 160-plus countries can trade without endless trade wars? The World Trade Organization, headquartered in Geneva.
p: The General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT), signed in 1947 and effective from 1948, governed world trade for decades. The Uruguay Round of negotiations led to the creation of the World Trade Organization (WTO), which came into being on 1 January 1995 as the successor to GATT.

The WTO is headquartered in Geneva, Switzerland. India is a founder member. Unlike GATT, the WTO is a permanent organisation with a legal status, and it covers trade in goods, services and intellectual property.

Objectives: to raise standards of living; to ensure full employment and growth in real income and effective demand; to expand production and trade in goods and services; to ensure optimal use of the world's resources; to protect the environment and promote sustainable development; to help developing countries get a fair share of growth in world trade; and to reduce tariffs and other trade barriers and eliminate discrimination.
Note: the complexities of international business, export promotion incentives and support organisations, and export processing zones were removed in rationalisation and are not covered here.

ex.q: Name the year the WTO was established and the organisation it replaced.
st: The Uruguay Round led to the WTO.
It began functioning on 1 January 1995.
It succeeded GATT.
ex.a: 1995; it replaced GATT.

topics.rl: India uses the WTO's dispute settlement process when it believes another country's trade rules hurt Indian exports, and defends its own policies there too.

rv.summary: The WTO, successor to GATT, came into being on 1 January 1995 after the Uruguay Round and is based in Geneva. It is a permanent body covering goods, services and IP, aiming to expand trade, raise living standards and reduce trade barriers.

qa.q: Which of these is an example of a non-economic activity?
qa.a: A teacher volunteering to teach children at a community centre free on Sundays
qa.e: An activity done for social or sentimental reasons, without the aim of earning money, is non-economic.

qa.q: Ravi sells his old laptop to a friend once. Which feature of business is missing?
qa.a: Regularity of dealings
qa.e: There is a sale, but it happens only once. Business needs dealings on a regular basis.

qa.q: Business is best described as an activity involving
qa.a: regular production or purchase and sale of goods and services to earn profit
qa.e: The definition combines production/purchase, sale or exchange, regularity and the profit motive.

qa.q: Why is risk called an inseparable element of business?
qa.a: Because business depends on uncertain future factors such as demand, prices and competition
qa.e: Every business decision is made today for an uncertain tomorrow, so the possibility of loss can never be fully removed.

qa.q: Which of the following is NOT a feature of business?
qa.a: Guaranteed and fixed return
qa.e: Business returns are uncertain; a fixed, guaranteed return is a feature of employment, not business.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Production of goods for self-consumption is not a business activity. Reason (R): Business involves sale or exchange of goods and services for value.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true. Goods made for own use are not sold or exchanged, and that is exactly why the activity is not business.

qa.q: A new cement plant in a backward district hires 800 local people and buys from local transporters. Which role of business does this mainly show?
qa.a: Generating employment and income that support economic development
qa.e: Business creates jobs and incomes directly and indirectly, which raises demand and development in the region.

qa.q: Which pair correctly matches the activity with its type?
qa.a: Nurse working in a hospital for a salary: economic
qa.e: The nurse works to earn a living, so the activity is economic. The other three are wrongly labelled.

qa.q: What was a shreni in ancient Indian trade?
qa.a: A guild or association of merchants or craftsmen
qa.e: Shrenis were guilds that organised traders and artisans and regulated their conduct.

qa.q: Which ancient port was located in Bengal and served trade with the east?
qa.a: Tamralipti
qa.e: Tamralipti was the great port of Bengal on the east coast.

qa.q: Kaveripatnam (Puhar) was an important port of which kingdom?
qa.a: Chola
qa.e: Kaveripatnam, at the mouth of the Kaveri, was a Chola port in the south.

qa.q: Which natural factor helped sailors plan voyages between India and West Asia?
qa.a: Seasonal monsoon winds
qa.e: Sailors timed their trips with the seasonal reversal of monsoon winds over the Arabian Sea.

qa.q: A guild fixes quality standards and penalises members who cheat buyers. This shows the guild's role in
qa.a: self-regulation of trade
qa.e: Guilds regulated their own members through rules, standards and penalties.

qa.q: Which of these was an inland trade centre rather than a port?
qa.a: Ujjain
qa.e: Ujjain in central India was an inland commercial centre; the others were ports.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Rivers played an important part in internal trade in ancient India. Reason (R): Water transport was cheaper and easier for carrying bulky goods between towns.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true, and the ease and low cost of moving bulky goods by water explains why rivers mattered for trade.

qa.q: The Silk Route mainly connected India with
qa.a: China, Central Asia and lands further west
qa.e: The Silk Route was a web of overland routes across Asia towards Europe.

qa.q: What was a hundi?
qa.a: An indigenous written instrument used for credit and remittance of money
qa.e: A hundi was a written order to pay money, used to finance trade and transfer funds.

qa.q: Which hundi is payable to any person, with no responsibility over who receives the payment?
qa.a: Dhani-jog
qa.e: Dhani-jog hundi can be paid to anyone who presents it.

qa.q: A hundi is payable only to a well-known, respectable person whose identity must be confirmed. It is a
qa.a: Shah-jog hundi
qa.e: 'Shah' refers to a respectable person; payment is made only to such an identified person.

qa.q: Firman-jog hundi is payable
qa.a: to order
qa.e: Firman-jog hundi is payable to the person named or as ordered.

qa.q: Why did hundis become popular with traders?
qa.a: They allowed money to be transferred and credit given without physically carrying cash over long distances
qa.e: Carrying cash over long routes was risky; a trusted paper order solved that problem.

qa.q: Commission agents and brokers became important in ancient trade mainly because they
qa.a: financed trade and bore risks while linking producers to distant buyers
qa.e: Intermediaries provided finance, took risks and connected markets.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Under a Jokhmi hundi, the drawee is not liable to pay if the goods are lost in transit. Reason (R): A Jokhmi hundi is drawn against goods dispatched, so payment depends on the goods reaching safely.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true; payment is linked to the safe arrival of goods, which explains why the drawee is free if they are lost.

qa.q: Which feature made the hundi a negotiable instrument?
qa.a: It could be transferred from one holder to another
qa.e: Negotiability means the right to receive payment can pass to another person by transfer.

qa.q: Which of the following was a major import of ancient India?
qa.a: Horses
qa.e: India imported horses, while indigo, spices and muslin were exports.

qa.q: Which group lists only ancient Indian exports?
qa.a: Spices, indigo, textiles
qa.e: Spices, indigo and textiles were exported; horses, gold, silver and wine were imported.

qa.q: How did colonial rule change India's role in world trade?
qa.a: India became mainly a supplier of raw materials and a market for British manufactured goods
qa.e: Colonial policy pushed India towards exporting raw materials and importing finished goods, hurting local industry.

qa.q: The economic reforms introduced in India in 1991 are usually summed up as
qa.a: Liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation
qa.e: The 1991 reforms opened the economy to markets, private firms and global trade.

qa.q: Ancient India imported gold and silver mainly because
qa.a: it had a trade surplus and received precious metals in payment for its goods
qa.e: Foreign buyers paid for Indian goods with precious metals, so gold and silver flowed into India.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Indian handicraft industries declined during colonial rule. Reason (R): Cheap machine-made British goods flooded Indian markets while India was turned into a raw-material supplier.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true; competition from factory goods and colonial trade policy explain the decline of crafts.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Indigo was an important import of ancient India. Reason (R): India had fertile land suited to growing many cash crops.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: Indigo was an export, not an import, so A is false. R is a true statement.

qa.q: Which statement about India's position in the world economy is correct?
qa.a: For centuries India was among the largest economies before declining under colonial rule
qa.e: India's share of world output was large before colonial rule; it declined and later recovered after reforms.

qa.q: What is the reward in a profession?
qa.a: Professional fee
qa.e: Professionals such as doctors and lawyers charge a fee for their services.

qa.q: In which occupation is transfer of interest possible?
qa.a: Business
qa.e: A business can be sold or transferred with some formalities; a professional's or employee's work cannot be transferred.

qa.q: Which occupation requires membership of a professional body to begin?
qa.a: Profession
qa.e: A profession starts with membership of a body like the Bar Council or ICAI and a certificate of practice.

qa.q: In which occupation is risk lowest?
qa.a: Employment
qa.e: Employees get fixed, regular pay, so risk is little or none.

qa.q: Which occupation needs no capital investment?
qa.a: Employment
qa.e: An employee simply works for an employer; no capital is invested.

qa.q: Nidhi has a law degree and is enrolled with the State Bar Council. She now takes up a job in a company's legal department on a monthly salary. Her present occupation is
qa.a: employment
qa.e: The deciding factor is how she works and is paid now: for an employer on a salary, which is employment.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A professional must follow a code of conduct. Reason (R): Professions are regulated by professional bodies that set standards of conduct for members.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true; the professional body lays down the code, which is why members must follow it.

qa.q: Which basis of comparison is correctly matched for employment?
qa.a: Mode of establishment: appointment letter and service agreement
qa.e: An employee joins through an appointment letter and service agreement. The other options describe business or profession.

qa.q: A fish hatchery that breeds fish for sale is an example of
qa.a: genetic industry
qa.e: Breeding animals for reproduction and sale is genetic industry; catching fish from the sea would be extractive.

qa.q: Which type of manufacturing separates a single material into different products?
qa.a: Analytical
qa.e: Analytical industry breaks a material into components, as an oil refinery does with crude oil.

qa.q: A firm puts together engines, bodies and tyres made by others to produce cars. This is
qa.a: assembling industry
qa.e: Assembling industry combines ready components into a finished product.

qa.q: Sugar and paper are produced through successive stages. These belong to
qa.a: processing industry
qa.e: Processing industry takes raw material through a series of stages to the final product.

qa.q: Building roads, bridges and dams falls under
qa.a: construction, a secondary industry
qa.e: Construction is part of secondary industry alongside manufacturing.

qa.q: Which of these is a tertiary (service) industry?
qa.a: Warehousing
qa.e: Warehousing supports trade and industry with storage services.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Mining is an extractive industry. Reason (R): Extractive industries draw products from natural sources.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true; mining extracts minerals from the earth, which is exactly what defines extractive industry.

qa.q: Raju runs a mango orchard nursery where he grows saplings and sells them to farmers. His business is
qa.a: genetic industry
qa.e: Raising plants for further reproduction and sale is genetic industry.

qa.q: Commerce consists of
qa.a: trade and auxiliaries to trade
qa.e: Commerce is trade plus the support services (auxiliaries) that help trade.

qa.q: Which auxiliary removes the hindrance of time?
qa.a: Warehousing
qa.e: Warehousing stores goods until they are needed, bridging the time gap between production and consumption.

qa.q: Importing goods for the purpose of re-exporting them is called
qa.a: entrepot trade
qa.e: Entrepot trade is import for re-export.

qa.q: Insurance helps commerce by removing the hindrance of
qa.a: risk
qa.e: Insurance protects traders against loss from fire, theft or accidents.

qa.q: A wholesaler who buys in bulk from manufacturers and sells to retailers within India is engaged in
qa.a: internal trade
qa.e: Buying and selling within the country is internal trade.

qa.q: Which of these is NOT an auxiliary to trade?
qa.a: Mining
qa.e: Mining is a primary (extractive) industry, not a support service to trade.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Advertising is an auxiliary to trade. Reason (R): Advertising removes the hindrance of information by telling buyers about products.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true; by informing customers it helps trade, which is why it is an auxiliary.

qa.q: Banks help commerce mainly by removing the hindrance of
qa.a: finance
qa.e: Banks provide funds and payment facilities to traders.

qa.q: Why can profit not be the only objective of business?
qa.a: Because a business has to balance several needs and interests, such as market standing, innovation and social responsibility, to survive and grow
qa.e: Over-focus on profit can harm customers, workers and long-run survival, so multiple objectives are needed.

qa.q: A firm compares its sales with those of its rivals and aims to become the market leader. This objective is
qa.a: market standing
qa.e: Market standing refers to a firm's position relative to its competitors.

qa.q: Productivity is best measured by comparing
qa.a: output with input
qa.e: Productivity = value of output relative to value of inputs used.

qa.q: Which of the following is a social objective of business?
qa.a: Providing employment opportunities
qa.e: Employment generation benefits society; the others are economic objectives.

qa.q: Profit is a 'reward for risk' because
qa.a: the businessman invests capital and bears the risk of loss in an uncertain environment
qa.e: Profit compensates the entrepreneur for taking the risk of uncertain returns.

qa.q: A pharma company spends heavily on research to develop new medicines. Which key-area objective is it pursuing?
qa.a: Innovation
qa.e: Developing new products and methods is innovation.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Earning profit is essential for the survival and growth of business. Reason (R): Retained profits provide funds for expansion and help the firm face difficult times.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true; profit provides the funds that allow survival and growth, so R explains A.

qa.q: Which of these is NOT one of Drucker's key areas for business objectives?
qa.a: Lowering taxes paid
qa.e: The key areas are market standing, innovation, productivity, physical and financial resources, profits, manager and worker performance, and social responsibility.

qa.q: Which of the following is a pure risk?
qa.a: Loss due to theft
qa.e: Theft can only cause loss; the others may cause gain or loss and are speculative.

qa.q: A sudden rise in interest rates increases a firm's borrowing cost. This is an example of a(n)
qa.a: economic cause of risk
qa.e: Interest rate changes are economic causes of business risk.

qa.q: Which statement about the nature of business risk is correct?
qa.a: The degree of risk depends mainly on the nature and size of the business
qa.e: Bigger businesses and certain lines of business face greater risks.

qa.q: Negligence by an employee that leads to damage of goods is a
qa.a: human cause of risk
qa.e: Dishonesty, carelessness and negligence of employees are human causes.

qa.q: Which risk offers a chance of both profit and loss?
qa.a: Speculative risk
qa.e: Speculative risk, such as price changes, can go either way.

qa.q: A garment exporter loses money because the rupee value changes against the dollar. This cause is classified as
qa.a: other causes (exchange-rate fluctuation)
qa.e: Exchange-rate fluctuations fall under 'other causes' along with political disturbances and mechanical failures.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Risk is an essential part of every business. Reason (R): Business decisions are made today for an uncertain future.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true; because the future is uncertain, every business carries risk.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Higher the risk, higher is generally the chance of profit. Reason (R): Profit is the reward for risk taking.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true; profit rewards risk, so those who bear more risk generally expect higher profit.

qa.q: Arranging machines, equipment and work stations on the factory floor is called
qa.a: plant layout
qa.e: Plant layout is the physical arrangement of facilities in the workplace.

qa.q: Which basic factor deals with estimating fixed and working capital needs?
qa.a: Financing the proposition
qa.e: Financing involves estimating capital needs and arranging sources.

qa.q: The first basic decision when starting a business is usually
qa.a: selection of the line of business
qa.e: You must first decide what kind of product or service to offer.

qa.q: A bakery owner chooses a shop near a college, close to her target customers. Which factor is she considering?
qa.a: Location
qa.e: Deciding where to set up near customers is the location decision.

qa.q: Why is tax planning listed as a basic factor in starting a business?
qa.a: Because tax laws affect decisions such as form of ownership, location and investment
qa.e: Taxes influence almost every decision, so they must be considered at the start.

qa.q: Which factor is concerned with whether the business will be a sole proprietorship, partnership or company?
qa.a: Choice of form of ownership
qa.e: This choice decides liability, control and capital-raising ability.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Location of a business should be decided carefully. Reason (R): A wrong location can raise costs and is difficult to change later.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true; because relocating is costly and hard, careful choice is needed.

qa.q: Which of these is NOT one of the basic factors in starting a business?
qa.a: Fixing the dividend for the next ten years
qa.e: Dividend policy is not among the basic start-up factors.

qa.q: Which form of business is owned, managed and controlled by one individual?
qa.a: Sole proprietorship
qa.e: 'Sole' means only one; one person owns, manages and controls it.

qa.q: The liability of a sole proprietor is
qa.a: unlimited
qa.e: His personal assets can be used to pay business debts.

qa.q: Shabnam's boutique has debts of ₹8,00,000 and business assets of ₹5,50,000. How much can creditors recover from her personal property?
qa.e: Unlimited liability: the shortfall of business assets is recovered from personal assets.

qa.q: Why does a sole proprietorship lack business continuity?
qa.a: Because the business and owner are not separate, so the owner's death, illness or insanity can end it
qa.e: With no separate entity, the business depends on the owner's life and capacity.

qa.q: In a sole proprietorship, the owner and the business are
qa.a: one and the same in the eyes of law
qa.e: There is no separate legal entity; the owner is held responsible for all business activities.

qa.q: Which of these is NOT a feature of sole proprietorship?
qa.a: Perpetual succession
qa.e: Perpetual succession is a feature of a company, not a sole proprietorship.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A sole proprietor enjoys complete control over the business. Reason (R): All decisions in a sole proprietorship are taken by the owner alone.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true; because the owner alone decides, he has complete control.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A sole proprietorship has a separate legal entity from its owner. Reason (R): A sole proprietor has unlimited liability.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: there is no separate entity. R is true: liability is unlimited.

qa.q: Which merit of sole proprietorship arises because the owner need not consult anyone?
qa.a: Quick decision making
qa.e: With no one else to consult, the owner decides and acts fast.

qa.q: 'Direct incentive' as a merit of sole proprietorship means that
qa.a: the owner directly gets all the profits, which motivates hard work
qa.e: There is a direct link between effort and reward since all profit is the owner's.

qa.q: Which is a limitation of sole proprietorship?
qa.a: Limited managerial ability
qa.e: One person may lack expertise in all areas of management.

qa.q: Sole proprietors find it hard to expand mainly because of
qa.a: limited resources
qa.e: Funds come only from the owner's savings and borrowings.

qa.q: Unlimited liability makes a sole proprietor
qa.a: cautious and reluctant to take big risks
qa.e: Fear of losing personal assets discourages bold, risky expansion.

qa.q: Which type of business is best suited to sole proprietorship?
qa.a: A small neighbourhood beauty parlour needing personal attention
qa.e: Small businesses with limited capital needs and personal service suit sole proprietorship.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A sole proprietor enjoys confidentiality of information. Reason (R): A sole proprietor is not required by law to publish his business accounts.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true; since accounts need not be published, information stays confidential.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Sole proprietorship has unlimited life. Reason (R): Sole proprietorship is easy to form and close.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: its life is limited. R is true: formation and closure are easy.

qa.q: Who manages a Joint Hindu Family business?
qa.a: The karta
qa.e: The eldest member, the karta, manages and controls the business.

qa.q: The liability of coparceners other than the karta is
qa.a: limited to their share in the family property
qa.e: Only the karta has unlimited liability.

qa.q: Membership in an HUF business is acquired by
qa.a: birth in the family
qa.e: No agreement is needed; one becomes a member by birth.

qa.q: The Dayabhaga system of inheritance prevails in
qa.a: West Bengal
qa.e: Dayabhaga prevails in West Bengal; Mitakshara prevails in the rest of India.

qa.q: Which is a merit of the HUF business?
qa.a: Continued business existence even after the karta's death
qa.e: The next eldest member takes over as karta.

qa.q: 'Dominance of karta' is a limitation of HUF business because
qa.a: the karta manages alone and may not accept the views of other members, causing conflict
qa.e: Unchecked control by one person can lead to conflicts and poor decisions.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A minor can be a member of a Joint Hindu Family business. Reason (R): Membership in an HUF business is by birth.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true; since birth makes one a member, minors are included.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The karta of an HUF has limited liability. Reason (R): The karta manages the HUF business.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: the karta's liability is unlimited. R is true.

qa.q: Which Act governs partnership firms in India?
qa.a: The Indian Partnership Act, 1932
qa.e: Partnerships are governed by the Indian Partnership Act, 1932.

qa.q: 'Mutual agency' in partnership means
qa.a: every partner is both an owner and an agent, so the act of one binds all
qa.e: Each partner represents the firm and the others in business dealings.

qa.q: The minimum number of members required to form a partnership is
qa.e: A partnership needs at least two persons who agree to share profits.

qa.q: As per the Companies Act, 2013 and its rules, the maximum number of partners in a partnership firm is
qa.e: Section 464 of the Companies Act, 2013 lets the government prescribe a limit of up to 100 partners; the Companies (Miscellaneous) Rules, 2014 fix it at 50.

qa.q: 'Joint and several' liability of partners means that
qa.a: partners are liable together, and each can also be held personally liable for all the firm's debts
qa.e: A creditor may recover the firm's debt from all partners together or from any one of them.

qa.q: Why do partnership firms often suffer from lack of public confidence?
qa.a: Because they are not required to publish their accounts
qa.e: Without published reports, outsiders cannot easily judge the firm's soundness.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A partnership firm can raise more funds than a sole proprietorship. Reason (R): In a partnership, capital is contributed by a number of partners.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true; several partners contribute, so more funds are available.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A partnership firm enjoys perpetual succession. Reason (R): Partnership is formed by an agreement among partners.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: retirement, death or insolvency of a partner can end it. R is true.

qa.q: A partner who contributes capital and shares profits but does not take part in day-to-day management is a
qa.a: sleeping partner
qa.e: Sleeping (dormant) partners invest but stay out of management.

qa.q: Which partner contributes no capital and takes no share in profits but lends his name to the firm?
qa.a: Nominal partner
qa.e: The nominal partner only lends his name and goodwill.

qa.q: A minor admitted to the benefits of partnership must, on attaining majority, decide whether to become a partner within
qa.a: six months
qa.e: He has six months to give public notice of his decision.

qa.q: Mehul tells a bank officer that he is a partner of their firm, though he is not. The bank lends on that basis. Mehul is a
qa.a: partner by estoppel
qa.e: By his own conduct he represented himself as a partner, so he is liable to the bank.

qa.q: A firm formed to construct a particular flyover, ending when the flyover is completed, is a
qa.a: particular partnership
qa.e: A partnership for a specific project or period is a particular partnership.

qa.q: The liability of a minor admitted to the benefits of partnership is
qa.a: limited to his share of capital and profits in the firm
qa.e: A minor is not personally liable beyond his share in the firm.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A secret partner has unlimited liability. Reason (R): A secret partner's association with the firm is not disclosed to outsiders.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true. But secrecy does not explain his unlimited liability; it arises because he is a real partner.

qa.q: Which statement about a Limited Liability Partnership (LLP) is correct?
qa.a: It is a separate legal entity in which partners' liability is limited
qa.e: An LLP, under the LLP Act, 2008, combines partnership flexibility with limited liability and separate entity.

qa.q: The document containing the terms and conditions of a partnership is called the
qa.a: partnership deed
qa.e: The partnership deed is the written agreement among partners.

qa.q: Which of the following is usually NOT included in a partnership deed?
qa.a: Names of the firm's future customers
qa.e: The deed covers relations among partners, not customer lists.

qa.q: Under the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, registration of a partnership firm is
qa.a: optional
qa.e: Registration is optional, but non-registration has legal consequences.

qa.q: Which is a consequence of non-registration of a partnership firm?
qa.a: The firm cannot file a suit against third parties
qa.e: An unregistered firm loses the right to sue others, but can still be sued.

qa.q: The application for registration of a partnership firm must be signed by
qa.a: all the partners
qa.e: All partners (or their agents) must sign the application.

qa.q: Rahul, a partner in an unregistered firm, wants to sue his co-partner for his share of profits. Can he?
qa.a: No, a partner of an unregistered firm cannot sue the firm or other partners
qa.e: This is one of the disabilities of non-registration.

qa.q: Assertion (A): It is advisable to have a written partnership deed. Reason (R): A written deed provides evidence of the agreed terms and helps settle disputes.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true; a written deed avoids misunderstandings because the terms are on record.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Registration of a partnership firm is compulsory in India. Reason (R): An unregistered firm cannot file a suit against third parties.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: registration is optional. R is true and is one consequence of not registering.

qa.q: The main motive of a cooperative society is
qa.a: service to its members
qa.e: Cooperatives exist to serve members' common interests, not to maximise profit.

qa.q: Voting in a cooperative society follows the principle of
qa.a: one member, one vote
qa.e: Every member has an equal vote regardless of capital contributed.

qa.q: A cooperative society is registered under
qa.a: the Cooperative Societies Act, 1912 or a State Cooperative Societies Act
qa.e: Registration under the cooperative law gives it a separate legal entity.

qa.q: Which type of cooperative protects members from moneylenders by giving loans at low interest?
qa.a: Credit cooperative society
qa.e: Credit cooperatives provide easy credit at reasonable rates.

qa.q: Why do cooperatives often suffer from inefficient management?
qa.a: Because they cannot afford high salaries for professional managers and are run by elected members
qa.e: Managing committees of members may lack expertise, and resources limit professional hiring.

qa.q: Why are cooperatives especially suited to weaker sections of society?
qa.a: They let people with small means pool resources, cut out middlemen and gain bargaining power, with equal voting and limited liability
qa.e: Pooling small resources gives the strength of scale while equal voting protects every member.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A cooperative society enjoys stable existence. Reason (R): A cooperative society has a separate legal entity, so death or insolvency of a member does not affect it.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true; the separate legal entity is why it continues despite changes in membership.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Members of a cooperative society have unlimited liability. Reason (R): Membership of a cooperative is voluntary.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: liability is limited to capital contributed. R is true.

qa.q: 'Perpetual succession' of a company means that
qa.a: its existence is not affected by the death, insolvency or exit of members
qa.e: Members may change, but the company continues until it is wound up by law.

qa.q: A company is called an artificial person because it
qa.a: is created by law and can own property, enter contracts and sue in its own name, but has no physical body
qa.e: It enjoys legal rights like a person even though it is not a natural person.

qa.q: A shareholder holds 500 shares of ₹10 each on which ₹6 per share has been paid. What is the maximum further amount he can be asked to pay?
qa.e: Liability is limited to the unpaid amount on shares: ₹4 × 500 = ₹2,000.

qa.q: Which limitation of a company means that a few directors effectively control it?
qa.a: Oligarchic management
qa.e: Rule by a few is called oligarchy; shareholders are scattered and often inactive.

qa.q: Why can a company raise much larger capital than a partnership?
qa.a: It can invite large numbers of investors to buy its shares and has greater borrowing ability
qa.e: Scope for expansion comes from wide share ownership and creditworthiness.

qa.q: Which body manages a joint stock company?
qa.a: The board of directors elected by shareholders
qa.e: Shareholders elect directors, who manage the company.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Company form suffers from lack of secrecy. Reason (R): Companies are required to file and publish many reports and accounts as per law.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true; legal disclosure requirements are the reason secrecy is hard.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Shareholders of a company have unlimited liability. Reason (R): A company is a separate legal entity.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: liability is limited. R is true; in fact it is why members are not personally liable for the company's debts.

qa.q: The minimum number of members required to form a public company is
qa.e: A public company needs at least seven members.

qa.q: Which of the following is a feature of a private company?
qa.a: It prohibits invitation to the public to subscribe to its securities
qa.e: A private company cannot invite the public to buy its shares.

qa.q: A private company has 260 members, including 70 present and past employees. For the 200-member limit, how many members are counted?
qa.e: Present and past employees are excluded: 260 − 70 = 190.

qa.q: A private company that is a subsidiary of a public company is treated as
qa.a: a public company
qa.e: The Companies Act, 2013 treats such a subsidiary as a public company.

qa.q: Which is a privilege enjoyed by a private company?
qa.a: It need not issue a prospectus
qa.e: Since it cannot invite the public, it does not need a prospectus.

qa.q: In a One Person Company, a nominee is required in order to
qa.a: become the member if the sole member dies or becomes incapable
qa.e: The nominee ensures continuity of the OPC.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A One Person Company enjoys limited liability. Reason (R): A One Person Company is a separate legal entity from its single member.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true; being a separate entity is why the member's liability is limited.

qa.q: The minimum number of directors required in a public company is
qa.e: Public companies need at least three directors; private ones need two.

qa.q: The first stage in the formation of a company is
qa.a: promotion
qa.e: Promotion, the conceiving of the idea and initial steps, comes first.

qa.q: A promoter checks whether a project is technically possible, financially viable and economically sound. This function is
qa.a: conducting feasibility studies
qa.e: Feasibility studies cover technical, financial and economic aspects.

qa.q: Application for approval of the proposed name of a company is made to the
qa.a: Registrar of Companies
qa.e: The Registrar of Companies approves names and registers companies.

qa.q: Which of the following is a function of a promoter?
qa.a: Appointing bankers, auditors and legal advisers
qa.e: Appointing professionals to help in formation is a promoter function.

qa.q: A company comes into legal existence when
qa.a: the certificate of incorporation is issued
qa.e: The certificate of incorporation marks its birth as a legal entity.

qa.q: Which stage is needed only for a public company that wants to raise funds from the public?
qa.a: Capital subscription
qa.e: Private companies cannot invite the public, so public capital subscription applies to public companies.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A promoter conducts feasibility studies before forming a company. Reason (R): Not every business opportunity is technically possible or financially profitable.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true; because some ideas may fail, feasibility studies are done first.

qa.q: 'Fixing up signatories to the Memorandum of Association' means
qa.a: deciding the members who will sign the Memorandum as subscribers
qa.e: The promoter decides who will sign the Memorandum as the first members.

qa.q: The document that defines the objects of a company and its relationship with the outside world is the
qa.a: Memorandum of Association
qa.e: The MoA is the charter of the company and states its objects.

qa.q: Which MoA clause states the purpose for which the company is formed?
qa.a: Objects clause
qa.e: The objects clause lists the main and other objects.

qa.q: An act done by a company beyond its Memorandum of Association is
qa.a: ultra vires and void; it cannot be ratified even by all shareholders
qa.e: Acts outside the MoA are void from the start.

qa.q: The Articles of Association contain
qa.a: rules for the internal management of the company
qa.e: AoA are the bye-laws governing internal affairs.

qa.q: Which document is conclusive evidence that a company has been legally formed?
qa.a: Certificate of incorporation
qa.e: Once issued, the certificate of incorporation settles the company's legal existence.

qa.q: The statutory declaration filed for incorporation states that
qa.a: all legal requirements for registration have been complied with
qa.e: It is a declaration of compliance with the requirements of the Act.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The Articles of Association are subordinate to the Memorandum of Association. Reason (R): The Articles cannot contain anything that goes against the Memorandum.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true; the MoA is the supreme document, which is why AoA must conform to it.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Acts beyond the Articles but within the Memorandum can never be ratified. Reason (R): Acts beyond the Memorandum are void.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: such acts can be ratified by shareholders. R is true.

qa.q: Which form of business is easiest and cheapest to set up?
qa.a: Sole proprietorship
qa.e: It needs almost no legal formalities.

qa.q: A business needs large capital and perpetual existence. The most suitable form is
qa.a: joint stock company
qa.e: Companies can raise huge capital and enjoy perpetual succession.

qa.q: Which forms have unlimited liability of owners?
qa.a: Sole proprietorship and partnership
qa.e: Sole proprietors and partners are personally liable for business debts.

qa.q: If the owner wants complete control and secrecy, which form is preferable?
qa.a: Sole proprietorship
qa.e: One owner controls everything and need not publish accounts.

qa.q: A group of doctors wants to pool skills and capital, share profits and keep formalities low. The most suitable form is
qa.a: partnership
qa.e: A partnership suits professionals pooling skills with fewer formalities.

qa.q: Which basis correctly distinguishes a private company from a public company?
qa.a: Minimum members: 2 in a private company, 7 in a public company
qa.e: Both have limited liability and separate entity; members and transfer rules differ.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A cooperative society is suitable for people with limited means. Reason (R): A cooperative works on the principle of service and gives equal voting rights to members.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true; service motive and equality are why it suits weaker sections.

qa.q: Rohit is a sole proprietor. His business has grown, and he now needs more money and a person with marketing skills. The best next step is to
qa.a: form a partnership with a partner who brings capital and marketing skills
qa.e: A partnership overcomes limited resources and limited managerial ability.

qa.q: An economy in which both private and public sectors operate together is called a
qa.a: mixed economy
qa.e: India has a mixed economy.

qa.q: Which of the following belongs to the private sector?
qa.a: A cooperative society
qa.e: Cooperatives are owned by members, not by the government.

qa.q: Public sector enterprises are owned, managed and controlled by
qa.a: the central government, state governments or both
qa.e: Government ownership and control defines the public sector.

qa.q: Which is NOT a form of organisation of public enterprises?
qa.a: Partnership firm
qa.e: Public enterprises take one of the three listed forms; partnership is a private form.

qa.q: A 'public company' and a 'public sector enterprise' differ because
qa.a: a public company is privately owned and can invite the public to buy shares, while a public sector enterprise is government-owned
qa.e: 'Public' in public company refers to share ownership by the public, not government ownership.

qa.q: The role of public and private sectors in India is decided mainly through
qa.a: industrial policies of the government
qa.e: Industrial policy resolutions define which sector does what.

qa.q: Assertion (A): India is described as a mixed economy. Reason (R): In India, both privately owned and government-owned enterprises operate.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true; the coexistence of both sectors is what makes the economy mixed.

qa.q: Assertion (A): All enterprises in the private sector are companies. Reason (R): The private sector includes enterprises owned by individuals or groups.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: sole proprietors, partnerships and cooperatives are also private sector. R is true.

qa.q: Which is an example of a departmental undertaking?
qa.a: Indian Railways
qa.e: Railways is run as a department of the Ministry of Railways.

qa.q: Departmental undertakings are financed by
qa.a: annual appropriations from the government budget
qa.e: They are funded from the treasury and their revenue goes back to it.

qa.q: Employees of a departmental undertaking are
qa.a: government servants
qa.e: They are civil servants under government service rules.

qa.q: Which is a merit of departmental undertakings?
qa.a: High degree of public accountability
qa.e: Being directly under a ministry, they are accountable to Parliament and the public.

qa.q: A major limitation of departmental undertakings is
qa.a: delays in decision making due to red tape
qa.e: Bureaucratic procedures slow decisions.

qa.q: Departmental undertakings are most suitable for areas where
qa.a: national security or strategic control is important
qa.e: Close government control matters most in strategic sectors.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Departmental undertakings lack flexibility. Reason (R): They must follow government rules and procedures and need ministry approval for decisions.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true; rigid procedures and approvals cause the lack of flexibility.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A departmental undertaking can sue and be sued in its own name. Reason (R): A departmental undertaking is part of the government ministry.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: it has no separate legal entity. R is true.

qa.q: A statutory corporation is created by
qa.a: a Special Act of Parliament or a state legislature
qa.e: Its powers and functions are laid down in a special statute.

qa.q: Which is an example of a statutory corporation?
qa.a: Life Insurance Corporation of India
qa.e: LIC was set up under the LIC Act, 1956.

qa.q: Employees of a statutory corporation are
qa.a: recruited under the corporation's own rules and are not civil servants
qa.e: They are governed by the terms laid down in the Act and the corporation's regulations.

qa.q: Statutory corporations are said to have the power of the government and
qa.a: the operational flexibility of private enterprise
qa.e: This combination is their main idea.

qa.q: Which is a limitation of statutory corporations?
qa.a: Any change in their constitution requires an amendment of the Act by Parliament
qa.e: Amending a law is slow, so changes are difficult.

qa.q: Who has ultimate financial responsibility for a statutory corporation?
qa.a: The government
qa.e: It is wholly owned by the state, which bears ultimate financial responsibility.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A statutory corporation can enter into contracts in its own name. Reason (R): A statutory corporation is a body corporate with a separate legal entity.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true; its separate legal entity allows it to contract in its own name.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Statutory corporations always enjoy complete freedom from political interference. Reason (R): Statutory corporations are set up under a Special Act.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: political interference in major decisions is a known limitation. R is true.

qa.q: A government company is one in which the government holds at least what percentage of the paid-up share capital?
qa.e: The Companies Act, 2013 requires not less than 51%.

qa.q: A government company is registered under
qa.a: the Companies Act, 2013
qa.e: It is formed like any other company under the Companies Act.

qa.q: In a company, the central government holds 35% and two state governments hold 10% each. What is the total government holding?
qa.e: Holdings of the Centre and states are added: 35 + 10 + 10 = 55%. So it is a government company.

qa.q: Which is an example of a government company?
qa.a: Steel Authority of India Limited
qa.e: SAIL is registered under the Companies Act with majority government ownership.

qa.q: Why is a government company said to 'evade constitutional responsibility'?
qa.a: Because, unlike a department, it is not directly answerable to Parliament
qa.e: It is run by its own board under the Companies Act, so direct parliamentary scrutiny is weaker.

qa.q: Which is a merit of government companies?
qa.a: Autonomy in management decisions
qa.e: As separate companies, they take their own business decisions.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A government company can be established easily. Reason (R): Only the requirements of the Companies Act need to be met; no special law is required.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true; because no separate Act is needed, setting one up is relatively easy.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A company in which the central government holds 40% and a state government holds 20% is not a government company. Reason (R): The holdings of central and state governments can be combined to meet the 51% test.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: 40% + 20% = 60%, so it is a government company. R is true.

qa.q: Which form of public enterprise has no separate legal entity?
qa.a: Departmental undertaking
qa.e: A department is part of the ministry, not a separate body.

qa.q: Case: 'An enterprise is registered under the Companies Act; the central government holds 74% of its shares and the public holds the rest.' Identify the form.
qa.a: Government company
qa.e: Registration under the Companies Act with at least 51% government holding means a government company.

qa.q: Case: 'The enterprise is run by a ministry, its staff are civil servants and its revenue is paid into the treasury.' Identify the form.
qa.a: Departmental undertaking
qa.e: Ministry control, civil servants and treasury revenue are classic departmental features.

qa.q: Which form is created by a Special Act that lays down its powers and functions?
qa.a: Statutory corporation
qa.e: The Special Act is the defining feature.

qa.q: Employees of which form are civil servants?
qa.a: Departmental undertaking
qa.e: Only departmental employees are government servants.

qa.q: On the basis of finance, which statement is correct?
qa.a: A government company can raise funds from the capital market, while a department depends on budget allocations
qa.e: Companies can issue shares; departments use budget funds.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A government company is more flexible than a departmental undertaking. Reason (R): A government company has its own board and is free from many government procedures.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
