qa.a: Convenience in buying, as all needs are met under one roof
qa.e: Shoppers save time by buying everything in one place.

qa.q: Why are prices at departmental stores often higher?
qa.a: Because of high operating costs such as rent, services and staff
qa.e: High overheads are passed on in prices.

qa.q: 'Centralised purchasing and decentralised sales' in a departmental store means
qa.a: buying is done centrally for all departments, while each department sells separately
qa.e: Central buying gets economies; departments handle their own sales.

qa.q: A customer who needs a medicine urgently at night finds the departmental store too far. Which limitation is this?
qa.a: Inconvenient location
qa.e: Central locations are inconvenient for urgent needs.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Departmental stores enjoy economies of large-scale operations. Reason (R): They buy in large quantities directly from manufacturers.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true; bulk direct buying gives these economies.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Departmental stores provide a high level of personal attention to customers. Reason (R): Departmental stores deal with a very large number of customers.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: lack of personal attention is a limitation, partly because they serve so many customers. R is true.

qa.q: Chain stores have no bad debts because
qa.a: all sales are made on a cash basis
qa.e: Cash sales mean nothing is owed.

qa.q: If one branch of a chain store makes losses and others make profits, the overall risk is reduced. This merit is
qa.a: diffusion of risk
qa.e: Losses in one shop are offset by profits elsewhere.

qa.q: Which is a limitation of chain stores?
qa.a: Branch managers lack initiative because they follow head office instructions
qa.e: Central control limits local initiative.

qa.q: On the basis of location, which is correct?
qa.a: A departmental store is at a central place; chain stores are spread across many localities
qa.e: Departmental stores attract customers to a centre; chain stores go close to customers.

qa.q: On the basis of range of products, which is correct?
qa.a: Departmental stores offer a wide variety; chain stores deal in a limited range
qa.e: Variety is the hallmark of departmental stores.

qa.q: Which format sells at uniform fixed prices across all its outlets?
qa.a: Chain store
qa.e: Chain stores maintain uniform prices; departmental stores may offer discounts.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Chain stores can transfer goods from one branch to another. Reason (R): All branches are owned and controlled centrally by the same head office.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true; common ownership and control is why stock can be moved between branches.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Departmental stores sell strictly on a cash basis, while chain stores give credit. Reason (R): Departmental stores and chain stores are both large-scale retailers.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: it is chain stores that sell strictly for cash; departmental stores may give credit. R is true.

qa.q: Mail order houses sell goods mainly through
qa.a: the mail, with no direct personal contact with buyers
qa.e: Orders and goods are exchanged by post.

qa.q: Which goods are most suitable for mail order business?
qa.a: Standardised and graded goods that are easy to transport
qa.e: Such goods can be described in catalogues and shipped cheaply.

qa.q: Under VPP (value payable post), the buyer pays
qa.a: when the goods are delivered by the post office
qa.e: VPP collects payment on delivery.

qa.q: Which is a limitation of mail order houses?
qa.a: No after-sales services
qa.e: Sellers are far away, so after-sales service is difficult.

qa.q: Mail order business can reach customers anywhere that
qa.a: the postal service reaches
qa.e: Wide reach depends on postal coverage.

qa.q: Mail order houses face high promotion costs because
qa.a: they must rely on advertisements, catalogues and circulars to reach buyers
qa.e: Without shops, they depend on costly promotion.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Mail order business has no bad debts. Reason (R): Payment is received in advance or at the time of delivery through the post office.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true; no credit sales is why there are no bad debts.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Mail order houses provide easy credit facilities to buyers. Reason (R): There is no personal contact between buyers and sellers in mail order business.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: mail order houses generally give no credit. R is true.

qa.q: GST came into force in India on
qa.a: 1 July 2017
qa.e: GST was launched on 1 July 2017.

qa.q: GST is described as a 'destination-based' tax because
qa.a: tax revenue goes to the state where the goods or services are consumed
qa.e: Consumption state gets the tax.

qa.q: On a supply within the same state, the taxes levied are
qa.a: CGST and SGST
qa.e: Intra-state supply attracts CGST and SGST in equal shares.

qa.q: Goods worth ₹30,000 are sold from Delhi to Haryana at 18% GST. The IGST payable is
qa.e: Inter-state supply attracts IGST at the full rate: 18% of ₹30,000 = ₹5,400.

qa.q: Goods worth ₹60,000 are sold within Maharashtra at 18% GST. The CGST amount is
qa.e: Intra-state: CGST is half the rate, 9% of ₹60,000 = ₹5,400.

qa.q: Who chairs the GST Council?
qa.a: The Union Finance Minister
qa.e: The Union Finance Minister chairs the Council, which includes state finance ministers.

qa.q: Assertion (A): GST has replaced many indirect taxes such as VAT, service tax and central excise duty. Reason (R): GST was introduced to create a single, unified indirect tax system across India.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true; the aim of a unified system is why multiple taxes were subsumed.

qa.q: Assertion (A): IGST is levied on supplies within the same state. Reason (R): IGST applies to inter-state supplies and imports.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: intra-state supplies attract CGST and SGST. R is true.

qa.q: Input tax credit means
qa.a: deducting GST already paid on purchases from GST collected on sales
qa.e: ITC lets businesses pay tax only on value added.

qa.q: A trader buys goods for ₹40,000 + 18% GST and sells them for ₹50,000 + 18% GST. Net GST payable after ITC is
The 'cascading effect' that GST removes refers to
qa.a: tax being charged on tax already included in the price
qa.e: Earlier taxes were levied on prices that already included tax.

qa.q: GSTN is
qa.a: the IT network that runs the GST portal for registration, returns and payments
qa.e: GSTN is the technology backbone.

qa.q: A small dealer under the composition scheme
qa.a: pays tax at a low fixed rate on turnover and cannot claim input tax credit
qa.e: Composition dealers trade simplicity for losing ITC and cannot charge GST on bills.

qa.q: Which is a role of chambers of commerce like FICCI and CII in promoting internal trade?
qa.a: Pressing for harmonisation of taxes and better infrastructure
qa.e: They advocate for traders on taxes, transport and infrastructure.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Input tax credit removes the cascading effect of taxes. Reason (R): Under ITC, tax is effectively paid only on the value added at each stage.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true; taxing only value added is exactly why tax on tax disappears.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Taxpayers under the composition scheme can claim input tax credit. Reason (R): The composition scheme is meant for small taxpayers.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: they cannot claim ITC. R is true.

qa.q: In most states, a business that supplies only goods must register under GST once its aggregate turnover in a year crosses
qa.a: ₹40 lakh
qa.e: The general registration threshold for suppliers of goods is ₹40 lakh a year (₹20 lakh for service providers; lower in some special-category states).

qa.q: International business includes
qa.a: trade in goods and services plus movement of capital, personnel, technology and intellectual property across borders
qa.e: It is broader than international trade.

qa.q: The relationship between international trade and international business is that
qa.a: international trade is a part of international business
qa.e: Business includes trade plus other cross-border operations.

qa.q: A major reason for international business is
qa.a: unequal distribution of natural resources among countries
qa.e: Countries trade to get what they lack.

qa.q: A country with abundant cheap skilled labour specialises in labour-intensive services and exports them. This shows
qa.a: differences in labour productivity and production costs
qa.e: Cost and productivity advantages drive specialisation.

qa.q: An Indian company licensing its technology to a firm in Brazil is part of
qa.a: international business, but not international trade in goods
qa.e: Licensing technology is a form of international business beyond trade.

qa.q: Specialisation in international business means
qa.a: each country focuses on producing what it can produce most efficiently and trades for the rest
qa.e: Specialisation increases total output and gains from trade.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Countries cannot produce all goods equally well or cheaply. Reason (R): Natural resources, labour productivity and production costs differ among countries.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true; these differences explain why countries differ in what they can produce cheaply.

qa.q: Assertion (A): International business involves only the movement of goods across borders. Reason (R): International trade includes exports and imports of goods and services.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: it also involves capital, technology, people and intellectual property. R is true.

qa.q: Which is a difference between domestic and international business?
qa.a: International business involves different currencies and exchange-rate risk
qa.e: Different currencies are a key difference.

qa.q: Tourism and travel, transportation and business services traded across borders are called
qa.a: invisible trade (service trade)
qa.e: Services are intangible, so this is invisible trade.

qa.q: Investment in a foreign company's shares only to earn dividends, without control, is
qa.a: portfolio investment
qa.e: Portfolio investors seek returns, not control.

qa.q: A Japanese firm sets up and manages its own plant in Gujarat. This is
qa.a: foreign direct investment
qa.e: Direct investment in assets with control is FDI.

qa.q: Mobility of factors of production like labour and capital is
qa.a: more restricted across countries than within a country
qa.e: Immigration rules, controls and other barriers restrict cross-border movement.

qa.q: 'Customer heterogeneity' in international markets means
qa.a: customers in different countries differ in tastes, preferences, language and culture
qa.e: Firms must adapt to diverse customers abroad.

qa.q: Assertion (A): International business faces exchange-rate risk. Reason (R): Different countries use different currencies, whose relative values keep changing.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true; changing currency values cause exchange-rate risk.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Factors of production move as freely between countries as within a country. Reason (R): Countries impose restrictions on immigration and movement of capital.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: mobility is more restricted across countries. R is true and explains why.

qa.q: Earning foreign exchange through exports is a benefit of international business to
qa.a: nations
qa.e: It helps the country pay for its imports.

qa.q: A firm sells abroad because domestic competition is cut-throat and margins are thin. This benefit is
qa.a: a way out of intense competition in the domestic market
qa.e: Foreign markets offer an outlet from domestic competition.

qa.q: A firm uses surplus production capacity by exporting. This benefit is
qa.a: increased capacity utilisation
qa.e: Idle capacity is put to use.

qa.q: How does international business raise the standard of living of people?
qa.a: By giving access to a wider variety of goods and services, often at lower prices
qa.e: Trade widens consumer choice.

qa.q: Which is a benefit of international business to firms?
qa.a: Prospects for higher profits
qa.e: Higher profits accrue to firms; the others are national benefits.

qa.q: A company's sales stagnate as the home market becomes saturated. It enters foreign markets to keep growing. Which benefit is this?
qa.a: Prospects for growth
qa.e: Foreign markets offer new growth when home demand plateaus.

qa.q: Assertion (A): International business helps nations use their resources more efficiently. Reason (R): Countries specialise in producing goods they can make most efficiently and import the rest.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true; specialisation is how resources get used efficiently.

qa.q: Assertion (A): International business reduces employment opportunities in a country. Reason (R): International business improves growth prospects of a country.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: it improves employment potential. R is true.

qa.q: Which is the simplest mode of entering international business?
qa.a: Exporting and importing
qa.e: It needs the least involvement and investment.

qa.q: A firm sells abroad through an Indian export house instead of contacting foreign buyers itself. This is
qa.a: indirect exporting
qa.e: Using intermediaries is indirect exporting.

qa.q: A firm gets components made by a manufacturer in Vietnam as per its specifications. This is
qa.a: contract manufacturing
qa.e: Production by a contracted foreign firm to specifications is contract manufacturing.

qa.q: Which is a limitation of exporting?
qa.a: Packaging, transport and insurance costs make goods costlier abroad
qa.e: Added costs raise the final price.

qa.q: Which is a merit of contract manufacturing for the international firm?
qa.a: Large-scale production without investing in production facilities abroad
qa.e: The foreign firm uses existing local facilities.

qa.q: Which is a limitation of contract manufacturing for the local firm?
qa.a: It must sell the goods to the international firm at predetermined prices
qa.e: Prices and buyer are fixed by contract.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Exporting involves less risk than other modes of entry. Reason (R): The exporter does not need to invest in setting up operations in the foreign country.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true; no foreign investment means less money at risk.

qa.q: Assertion (A): In contract manufacturing, the international firm must build its own factory abroad. Reason (R): Contract manufacturing uses local manufacturers in foreign countries.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: it uses existing local factories. R is true.

qa.q: The fee paid by a licensee to a licensor for using its patents or know-how is called
qa.a: royalty
qa.e: Royalty is the payment for licensing.

qa.q: How does franchising differ from licensing?
qa.a: Franchising is used mainly for services, and the franchiser exercises stricter control
qa.e: Franchising transfers a whole business system for services.

qa.q: A major limitation of licensing for the licensor is that
qa.a: the licensee may later start selling a similar product and become a competitor
qa.e: Knowledge gained may be used to compete after the agreement ends.

qa.q: Which is a merit of a joint venture for a foreign firm?
qa.a: It benefits from the local partner's knowledge of markets, culture and politics
qa.e: Local partners reduce the risk of operating in an unfamiliar market.

qa.q: A parent company sets up a brand-new 100%-owned plant in a foreign country. This is a
qa.a: greenfield venture (wholly owned subsidiary)
qa.e: New 100%-owned operations abroad are greenfield ventures.

qa.q: Why is a wholly owned subsidiary not suitable for small and medium firms?
qa.a: Because the parent must invest 100% of the equity and bear all losses
qa.e: Full investment and full risk need big resources.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A wholly owned subsidiary need not disclose its technology to any partner. Reason (R): In a wholly owned subsidiary, the parent company holds 100% equity and full control.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true; full ownership is why no partner is involved to share secrets with.

qa.q: Rank the modes from least to most investment: joint venture, exporting, wholly owned subsidiary.
qa.a: Exporting → joint venture → wholly owned subsidiary
qa.e: Exporting needs the least investment; a WOS needs the most.

qa.q: A document sent by the exporter giving details of quality, size, price and terms of the goods, in reply to an enquiry, is the
qa.a: proforma invoice
qa.e: The proforma invoice acts as a quotation.

qa.q: The IEC number required for exporting is issued by the
qa.a: Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT)
qa.e: DGFT issues the Importer Exporter Code.

qa.q: Why does an exporter ask the importer for a letter of credit?
qa.a: To get a guarantee from the importer's bank that payment will be made
qa.e: It secures payment for the exporter.

qa.q: Finance obtained by an exporter from a bank to buy raw materials and produce goods for export is
qa.a: pre-shipment finance
qa.e: It is taken before goods are shipped.

qa.q: Which step comes immediately after receiving the order or indent?
qa.a: Assessing the importer's creditworthiness and securing a letter of credit
qa.e: Before investing in the order, the exporter checks payment safety.

qa.q: An exporter registers with the relevant Export Promotion Council and obtains a
qa.a: Registration-cum-Membership Certificate (RCMC)
qa.e: Registration with the EPC gives the RCMC.

qa.q: Assertion (A): An exporter should assess the importer's creditworthiness before producing goods. Reason (R): There is a risk that a distant foreign importer may not pay.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true; the payment risk is why creditworthiness is checked early.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The indent is sent by the exporter to the importer. Reason (R): An indent is an order placed for the goods.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: the indent is placed by the importer. R is true.

qa.q: The document issued by the captain of the ship acknowledging that the cargo has been loaded on board is the
qa.a: mate's receipt
qa.e: The mate's receipt is issued after loading.

qa.q: The main document on the basis of which customs grants permission to export is the
qa.a: shipping bill
qa.e: The shipping bill is filed for export customs clearance.

qa.q: A bill of lading is
qa.a: a document issued by the shipping company accepting goods for carriage, and a document of title
qa.e: It acknowledges goods for carriage and transfers title.

qa.q: Under a usance draft, the documents are released to the importer
qa.a: on acceptance of the bill of exchange (D/A)
qa.e: Usance means payment after a period, so documents go against acceptance.

qa.q: The certificate of origin helps the importer to
qa.a: claim tariff concessions or exemptions based on the country of manufacture
qa.e: Some countries give concessions on goods from certain nations.

qa.q: Which document instructs the ship's captain to receive specified goods on board?
qa.a: Shipping order
qa.e: The shipping order is issued after space is reserved.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The exporter gets the bill of lading after the mate's receipt. Reason (R): The shipping company issues the bill of lading in exchange for the mate's receipt after freight is paid.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true; the mate's receipt and freight payment lead to the bill of lading, so it comes later.

qa.q: Which is the correct sequence?
qa.a: Shipment inspection → customs clearance → mate's receipt → bill of lading
qa.e: Inspection comes before customs; loading (mate's receipt) comes before the bill of lading.

qa.q: Which is the first step in the import procedure?
qa.a: Trade enquiry
qa.e: The importer begins by gathering information and quotations.

qa.q: To obtain foreign exchange, an importer applies to
qa.a: a bank authorised by the RBI
qa.e: Authorised banks release foreign exchange as per rules.

qa.q: The form filled by the importer for customs, containing details of goods and assessment of import duty, is the
qa.a: bill of entry
qa.e: The bill of entry is the import customs document.

qa.q: 'Retirement of import documents' means
qa.a: paying or accepting the bill of exchange to obtain shipping documents from the bank
qa.e: Documents are 'retired' when the importer takes them up from the bank.

qa.q: A shipment advice is sent by
qa.a: the exporter to the importer after shipping the goods
qa.e: It informs the importer about the shipment.

qa.q: Which document does the importer need to take delivery of goods from the shipping company?
qa.a: Delivery order (against the bill of lading)
qa.e: The shipping company endorses delivery to the importer.

qa.q: Assertion (A): An importer must check the EXIM policy before importing goods. Reason (R): Some goods can be imported only with a licence, while others are freely importable.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true; differing licence requirements are why the policy must be checked.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The bill of entry is used for export customs clearance. Reason (R): The bill of entry contains details of goods for assessment of import duty.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: it is used for import clearance; the shipping bill is for exports. R is true.

qa.q: A bill of exchange payable immediately on presentation is a
qa.a: sight draft
qa.e: Sight means payable at sight.

qa.q: A bill of exchange payable after a specified period is a
qa.a: usance draft
qa.e: Usance drafts allow time for payment.

qa.q: Which document is a document of title to goods shipped by sea?
qa.a: Bill of lading
qa.e: The bill of lading can be transferred to pass title.

qa.q: In a bill of exchange used in export trade, the drawer is the
qa.a: exporter
qa.e: The exporter draws the bill on the importer.

qa.q: Which document is issued by the importer's bank?
qa.a: Letter of credit
qa.e: The LC is opened by the importer's bank in favour of the exporter.

qa.q: Which document is prepared by the exporter for customs clearance at the port of export?
qa.a: Shipping bill
qa.e: The shipping bill is the export customs document.

qa.q: Assertion (A): An airway bill is used instead of a bill of lading for air cargo. Reason (R): A bill of lading is issued for goods carried by sea.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true; since the bill of lading is for sea transport, air cargo needs an airway bill.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The indent is a quotation sent by the exporter. Reason (R): A proforma invoice gives details of goods and price in reply to an enquiry.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: the indent is the importer's order; the quotation is the proforma invoice. R is true.

qa.q: The WTO came into existence on
qa.a: 1 January 1995
qa.e: It started functioning on 1 January 1995.

qa.q: The WTO is the successor of
qa.a: GATT
qa.e: The WTO replaced the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade.

qa.q: The headquarters of the WTO is in
qa.a: Geneva
qa.e: It is located in Geneva, Switzerland.

qa.q: Which is an objective of the WTO?
qa.a: Ensuring optimal use of the world's resources
qa.e: Optimal resource use is a stated objective.

qa.q: How does the WTO differ from GATT?
qa.a: The WTO is a permanent organisation that also covers services and intellectual property
qa.e: The WTO has wider scope and a permanent legal status.

qa.q: The WTO helps developing countries mainly by
qa.a: working to ensure they get a fair share in the growth of world trade
qa.e: Special attention to developing countries is an objective.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The WTO aims to reduce tariffs and other barriers to trade. Reason (R): Lower trade barriers help expand trade in goods and services among member countries.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true; expanding trade is why the WTO seeks lower barriers.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The WTO was set up in 1948. Reason (R): GATT came into effect in 1948.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: the WTO came into being in 1995. R is true.
